name: Asset Security
plainMeaning: This domain is about knowing what valuable information and equipment you have and deciding how much protection each item needs. It also covers looking after each item from the day it is created or bought until it is safely destroyed.

topics.name: Identify and classify information and assets
topics.simpleExplanation: Not everything you own needs the same protection. At home, you lock your passport in a safe, but you leave a magazine on the table. Organizations do the same. First they find out what information and equipment they have. Then they put each item into a group, called a class, based on how much harm its loss would cause. Each class has its own protection rules. Money goes to what really matters, and nobody has to guess how to treat an item.

studyNotes.heading: Why we classify at all
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at why organizations sort their information into groups at all, because every later step in this domain depends on it.

Classification means sorting information by the harm that would follow if it were exposed, changed or lost. Each group is called a class. Each class comes with its own protection rules.

Think about your own home. Your passport goes in a safe. Your shopping list stays on the fridge. If you guarded both in the same way, you would either spend far too much protecting the list, or far too little protecting the passport. You already classify things without using the word.

Now think about a workplace. A bank holds customer account numbers, staff payroll, a public list of branch opening hours, and plans for a merger that nobody outside may know about. Treating all four the same would be wasteful and dangerous at once. The opening hours need almost nothing. The merger plans need a great deal.

This gives classification its main benefit. It makes the cost of protection match the value of what is protected. It gives staff clear instructions, so nobody has to guess. It helps leaders to spend money where the harm would be greatest. And it helps to show regulators, which are the official bodies that enforce rules, that the organization takes proper care of what it holds.

Classification looks at all three goals of security. Confidentiality means keeping information away from the wrong people. Integrity means keeping it correct. Availability means having it there when it is needed. Most class names focus on confidentiality, but a good program considers all three.

Here is one important warning. Classification is not a control by itself. A control is anything that reduces risk, such as a lock, a password or a rule. A label on a file stops nobody. It is a decision that tells us which controls to apply.

Here is what to take away. Classification sorts things by harm, it matches protection to value, and it tells people what to do. It is the decision that comes before the controls.

studyNotes.heading: Building a classification program, step by step
studyNotes.body:
Next we will walk through how an organization sets up classification, because the exam likes to ask what comes first and what comes next.

Imagine sorting a family's papers after moving house. First, the family agrees on the piles: keep safe, keep handy, throw away. Then someone finds all the boxes. Then someone decides which pile each paper belongs in. Only then do you buy the safe. A business works in much the same way.

A sensible order for a classification program is this.

- Step 1: Get senior management support and set the class levels in a policy.
- Step 2: Find the information and assets you have.
- Step 3: Name an owner for each one.
- Step 4: The owner assigns a class, using agreed criteria.
- Step 5: Apply the protection rules for that class.
- Step 6: Train staff and review the classes regularly.

Let us follow a hospital through those steps. The board approves a policy with three classes. Staff then search for information, including the forgotten copies on old file shares. Software called a data discovery tool helps, by searching storage for patterns such as patient numbers. The director of nursing is named owner of the ward records. She assigns them the highest class. The security team and the technical teams then apply the rules for that class. Staff are trained, and the owner looks at the class again each year.

Notice why senior management comes first. A classification program costs money and changes how people work. Without support from the top, it fades away within months.

Notice also that finding the information comes before deciding on controls. You cannot protect what you do not know you have. If an answer offers to buy a tool before you know what you hold, be suspicious of it.

Think like a manager here. Your job is to make sure the process exists and that the right people make the decisions. You are not there to label every file yourself.

Here is your takeaway. Policy and management support first, then find it, name an owner, classify, protect, train and review.

studyNotes.heading: Government classes and the idea of clearance
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at the class names used by the United States government, because the exam expects you to know them in order and to know what each one means.

From highest to lowest, the levels are these.

- Top Secret: disclosure could cause exceptionally grave damage to national security.
- Secret: disclosure could cause serious damage.
- Confidential: disclosure could cause damage.
- Unclassified: not covered by the three levels above.

The words to remember are grave, serious, and plain damage. Say them to yourself in that order. Exceptionally grave belongs to Top Secret. Serious belongs to Secret. Damage, with no extra word, belongs to Confidential.

Unclassified does not always mean free for anyone to read. The United States also uses a category called Controlled Unclassified Information, or CUI. This is information that is not classified, but which laws or policies still require to be protected.

Now we need a second idea. Information has a classification. A person has a clearance. A clearance is official approval, after a background check, to see information up to a certain level. But clearance alone is never enough. The person must also have a need to know, which means that their job really requires this particular information.

Think about a hotel. A staff key card may open every floor. That does not mean that a cook should be walking through guests' rooms. The card shows what the person could reach. The job decides where the person should go.

Here is a workplace example. A defense analyst holds a Secret clearance. A colleague on another project has a Secret report. The analyst's clearance is high enough. But the report has nothing to do with her work, so she has no need to know, and she should not read it.

This matters for the exam because a wrong answer will often say that the person's clearance is high enough, so access is fine. It is not fine unless the job requires it.

Here is what to take away. Know the order: Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, Unclassified. And remember that access needs clearance and need to know together.

studyNotes.heading: Business classes and how the owner decides
studyNotes.body:
Now we move from government to business, and we will look at who chooses a class and what they base the choice on.

Businesses have no single required scheme. A common one, from highest to lowest, is this.

- Confidential or Proprietary: trade secrets and the most valuable company data.
- Private: personal details about staff or customers.
- Sensitive: internal data that needs some care.
- Public: safe for anyone to see.

Watch the trap with these names. Confidential is the lowest of the three secret government levels, but it is often the top level in a company. When two organizations work together, or merge, the same word may mean very different things. The answer is to map one scheme to the other, in writing.

Keep the number of levels small. Three or four is common. Too many levels confuse people, and confused people make mistakes.

The person who chooses the class is the owner. The owner is a senior business person who answers for the information. Technical staff can advise, and they carry out the rules, but they do not decide. Think of a family deciding which papers go in the safe. The family decides, even though a locksmith fits the safe.

Owners use criteria such as these.

- Value: what it is worth to the organization.
- Sensitivity: the harm if the wrong people see it.
- Criticality: how much the business depends on it being correct and available.
- Legal and contract rules: for example, laws on personally identifiable information, or PII, which is any data that can point to a particular person.
- Age and useful life: value often falls over time.

Sensitivity and criticality are not the same thing. A hospital's bed schedule would embarrass nobody if it leaked, so its sensitivity is low. But wards cannot admit patients without it, so its criticality is high. Protected health information, or PHI, the medical data about a person, is usually high on both.

Think like a manager. Classifying too high wastes money, and staff stop taking the labels seriously. Classifying too low leaves valuable things exposed.

Here is your takeaway. The owner decides, using written criteria, and three or four clear levels work best.

studyNotes.heading: Classifying assets and the high-water mark
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will turn from the information itself to the things that hold it, and we will see the rule that decides their level.

Data classification is about the information, such as a customer list or a payroll file. Asset classification is about the things that hold or handle that information, such as laptops, servers, paper files and backup tapes. A server is a central computer that serves many users. The two go together, and the data comes first. You decide how sensitive the data is, and that tells you how to treat what it sits on.

The key rule is that an asset takes the class of the most sensitive information on it. This is often called the high-water mark. Think of the line that a flood leaves on a wall. It records the highest level the water reached, however low the water usually is.

Here is a worked example. A school laptop holds 500 public newsletters and one file of student medical notes. The medical notes are the highest class. So the whole laptop gets that level of protection. Counting files does not matter. One sensitive file sets the level. If the school wants a cheaper level for that laptop, it can move the medical file somewhere else.

Ask also where copies go. A test system loaded with real customer records holds real customer data, so it takes the same class, even if the project calls it low value. The safest fix is to test with made-up data instead.

Do not forget less obvious assets. Office printers often keep images of what they have scanned on an internal drive. Those printers hold whatever class they have copied.

You may also meet the word categorization. In United States government practice, a standard called Federal Information Processing Standard 199 groups systems as low, moderate or high impact. It looks separately at confidentiality, integrity and availability. The overall rating for the system then follows the highest of the three results. So categorization groups systems by impact, and classification labels information by sensitivity. They are close cousins, and the high-water idea appears in both.

Here is what to take away. The data sets the class, and one sensitive item lifts the whole asset to its level.

studyNotes.heading: Aggregation, inference, downgrading and review
studyNotes.body:
In this final part we will look at how a class can change, either because facts are combined, or because time has passed.

Start with aggregation. Aggregation means combining many low-value facts, so that together they become more sensitive. One delivery time for one truck is harmless. A full year of delivery times can reveal exactly when a cash shipment is easiest to rob. So the combined collection may need a higher class than any of its parts.

Inference is related, but it is different. Inference means working out a hidden fact from the facts you are allowed to see. Suppose a report shows only the total pay of each team. Last month a team had a total of 90,000 dollars. This month one person joined, and the total is 95,000 dollars. Now take 90,000 from 95,000. The answer is 5,000 dollars, and you have just learned the new person's monthly pay. Nobody showed it to you. You worked it out.

So aggregation is about the collection becoming sensitive. Inference is about deducing one protected fact.

Now think about time. A school exam paper is highly secret the day before the exam. A week later it may be public. People often call moving an item to a lower class declassification or downgrading. In strict government language, downgrading means moving to a lower level, while declassification means removing the classification altogether.

The decision belongs to the owner. A deadline, a cost problem or an awkward process is not a reason to lower a class. The only proper reason is that the harm of exposure has really fallen.

Here is a workplace example. A product launch plan was the company's most protected document for a year. The product is now on sale and its details are on the website. The owner reviews the plan, and lowers the class. Money is no longer spent guarding something that the whole world can read.

That is why classes need a regular review. Value changes, laws change, and data gets combined in new ways.

Here is your takeaway. Combining facts can raise a class, time can lower it, and the owner makes the call at a regular review.

keyTerms.meaning: Sorting information and assets into groups by the harm their loss or exposure would cause.
How much harm would follow if the wrong people saw the information.
How much the organization depends on the information or asset to keep working.
The rule that a system is protected at the level of the most sensitive information it holds.
Personally Identifiable Information: any data that can point to a particular person.
Combining many low-value facts so that together they become more sensitive.
Moving information to a lower class when it no longer needs so much protection.

keyPoints: Find what you have first, because you cannot protect what you do not know about.
The owner assigns the class, not the technical staff.
An asset takes the class of the most sensitive information it holds.
Classification makes the cost of protection match the value of the item.
Review classes regularly, because value changes over time.
topics.memoryHook: Passport in the safe, shopping list on the fridge: protect each thing by what it would cost you to lose it.

question.prompt: Senior management at a growing chain of shops has approved a new classification program and a policy setting the class levels. The security manager is planning the next stage. What should happen FIRST?
options: Buy labeling software so that each new file can be marked automatically
Find out what information and assets the company actually holds
Encrypt every file server so that the data stays safe during the project
Train all staff on how to handle each of the new classification levels
question.explanation: You cannot classify or protect what you have not found, so finding the information and assets comes next. Training is tempting, but staff need real classes and rules first. Software and encryption are controls, and controls are chosen after the classes are known.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An employee at a defense contractor holds a Secret clearance. He asks to read a Secret report from a project he does not work on, and says that his clearance already allows it. What is the BEST response?
options: Give him the report, because his clearance level matches the class of the report exactly
Refuse for now, because he has no need to know what is in a report for that project
Ask him to sign a confidentiality form and then give him a printed copy of the report
Raise his clearance to Top Secret so that the same question does not come up again
practiceQuestions.explanation: Access needs both clearance and need to know, and his job does not require this report. Handing it over is tempting because the levels match, but matching levels are only half of the test. A form or a higher clearance does not create a need to know.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two companies are merging. In one, Confidential is the highest class. In the other, Confidential is a middle class and Restricted is the highest. Staff have begun sharing files between the two. What would BEST prevent mishandling?
options: Tell all staff to treat shared files as Public until the merger is complete and the policies agree
Let each company go on using its own meaning of the words for as long as it wishes to do so
Rename every class in both companies to a number so that nobody is confused by the old words
Map the two schemes to each other in an approved policy, and tell staff how they line up
practiceQuestions.explanation: A written mapping tells people exactly how a class in one company translates into the other. Renaming the classes is tempting, but numbers alone do not say which level equals which. Treating files as Public under-protects them.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A logistics firm publishes each delivery in a separate public notice. An analyst combines a full year of notices and finds that the collection reveals the exact routine of its cash shipments. Each single notice is harmless. What is the BEST response?
options: Have the owner review the combined collection and assign it a higher class than its parts
Leave it as it is, because each single notice that went into it was already classed as Public
Delete the analyst's work and ask the analyst not to combine public information in the future
Make every individual notice Top Secret so that nobody can ever combine them again in any form
practiceQuestions.explanation: This is aggregation, where a combined collection becomes more sensitive than its parts, so the collection needs its own higher class. Leaving it alone is tempting because each part is public, but the harm comes from the combination. Raising every single notice is out of proportion.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A staff portal shows only the total pay of each small team, and a list of who joined each team this month. An employee compares last month's total with this month's and works out the exact pay of a new colleague. Which problem does this show MOST clearly?
options: Data remanence, because old pay data was left behind
Aggregation, because many records are held in one place
Inference, because a protected fact was worked out
Declassification, because the pay data was moved down
practiceQuestions.explanation: Inference means deducing a hidden fact from facts you are allowed to see. Aggregation is tempting, but aggregation describes a collection becoming sensitive, and here one particular protected fact was worked out.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A new product plan was given a company's highest class before launch. The product launched six months ago, and the details are now on its website. The plan is still stored under the strictest and most costly controls. What is the BEST next step?
options: Leave the class unchanged, because a class once given should never be lowered by anybody
Ask the owner to review the class, and to lower it if the harm has really fallen
Let the storage administrator lower the class now, in order to reduce this quarter's costs
Delete the plan right away, since all of its contents have already been made public
practiceQuestions.explanation: Value falls over time, and the owner is the person who may change a class. It is tempting to let the administrator act, since the saving is real, but technical staff carry out class decisions and do not make them. Deleting it ignores any retention need.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An audit finds that nearly every document in a company is marked at the highest class. Staff admit that they ignore the markings and email these files freely. What is the BEST corrective action?
options: Have the owners reclassify items against clear criteria, and then retrain the staff on them
Discipline every employee who emailed a marked file and make them sign the policy once again
Buy stronger encryption for all documents, because all of them are marked at the highest class
Remove all of the markings, since the staff have already shown that they do not read them
practiceQuestions.explanation: Over-classification is the cause, because staff stop believing the labels when everything is top level. Discipline is tempting, but it punishes the symptom and leaves the broken scheme in place. Encryption would spend more money on the same mistake.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A finance director asks why the company should spend time on a classification program when it already has good firewalls, which filter network traffic. What is the BEST answer from the security manager?
options: It removes the need for most other controls, because a labeled file cannot be misused by staff
It is a technical requirement of every modern firewall and cannot be avoided by any company
It places every item under the same strong level of protection, which makes the rules much simpler
It lets the company match its protection spending to the value of each item that it holds
practiceQuestions.explanation: The main business benefit is matching the cost of protection to the value of what is protected, which is language a finance director can use. Equal protection for everything sounds simple, but it is the exact waste that classification is meant to avoid.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Developers copied the live customer database to a test system so that they could try a new feature with realistic data. The test system has weak controls, because the project labeled it as low value. What is the BEST action?
options: Keep the test system as it is, since test systems are by definition low in value and low in risk
Ask the developers to promise not to look at any of the customer details while they test the feature
Protect it at the customer data's class, or replace the real data with made-up values
Move the test system to a different building so that it is further away from the live database
practiceQuestions.explanation: A copy keeps the class of the data it holds, whatever a project calls the system. Replacing the real data removes the problem, and protecting it properly also meets the rule. A promise from the developers is tempting because it is cheap, but it is not a control over the data.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A hospital's bed-scheduling data would embarrass nobody if outsiders saw it. However, wards cannot admit patients if the data is wrong or unavailable. Which factor should MOST drive the protection of this data?
options: Criticality, because the hospital depends on it
Sensitivity, because outsiders might read it
Age, because schedules soon go out of date
Marking, because schedules must carry a banner
practiceQuestions.explanation: Criticality measures how much the organization depends on data being correct and available. Sensitivity is tempting because it is the factor most often discussed, but the scenario says that exposure would cause little harm.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A government analyst is reviewing a new report. Its unauthorized disclosure could reasonably be expected to cause serious damage to national security, but not exceptionally grave damage. Which United States classification level fits BEST?
options: Top Secret
Secret
Confidential
Unclassified
practiceQuestions.explanation: Serious damage is the test for Secret. Top Secret is tempting because the report is clearly important, but it is reserved for exceptionally grave damage. Confidential is for damage without the word serious.

topics.name: Information and asset handling requirements: marking, labeling, storage, transport
topics.simpleExplanation: Once something has a class, people need to know how to treat it. Handling rules say exactly that. Think of a bank moving cash. The bags are marked, the cash sits in a vault, and an armored van carries it with a signature at each stop. Information needs the same care. It is marked so people know its class. It is stored safely. It is moved safely. The rules for each class are written down, so that staff never have to guess.

studyNotes.heading: What handling requirements are
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at what handling rules are and where they come from.

A handling requirement is a written rule that says how people must treat an item of a given class. The rules cover the item at every moment: when it is marked, used, stored, moved, copied and thrown away.

Think about medicine in a family home. The label tells you what it is. The strong tablets go on a high shelf, out of reach of children. You carry them home in a closed bag. When they expire, you take them back to the pharmacy and you do not tip them in the bin. Each stage has its rule, and the rule depends on how dangerous the medicine is.

Now think about a law firm. It might have three classes. Public items may go anywhere. Internal items stay within the firm's systems. Client Confidential items must be encrypted, may be seen only by the people working on that case, and must be shredded when they are finished with. Encryption means scrambling data so that only someone with the key can read it. A person who picks up a file needs only to see the class to know what the rules are.

The rules come from policy, and policy needs management support. Under the policy sit standards and procedures, which spell out the exact steps. Staff then need training, because a rule that nobody knows protects nothing.

The most important idea in this topic is that protection must stay with the information. A secret stays a secret when it is printed, emailed, photographed or copied to a backup. A backup needs the same protection as the original. A printout of a confidential report is still confidential, even if it is just lying on a desk.

Think like a manager. If three departments treat the same class in three different ways, the people are not the problem. The missing written rule is the problem, and that is what you fix.

Here is what to take away. Handling rules are written per class, they cover the whole life of the item, and the protection follows the information wherever it goes.

studyNotes.heading: Marking and labeling
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at how people and computers can tell what class an item belongs to.

Marking and labeling both show the class of an item. Many people use the two words to mean the same thing. In the more exact language of United States government security standards, marking is what people can read, such as a stamp on a page. A label is often a tag held inside the system that computers can read and act on.

Think about food in a shop. The words on the packet are for you to read. The barcode is for the machine at the till. Both describe the same product, and each serves a different reader.

Items should be marked in every form they take.

- Paper: the class at the top and bottom of each page.
- Screens: a banner that shows the class.
- Files and emails: a tag in the file details or a note in the subject line.
- Removable media: a physical sticker.

Removable media means storage that you can carry, such as tapes and disks. The file details just mentioned are often called metadata, which means data about data, such as the author or the date.

The computer-readable tag matters more every year. Automated tools can only act on a class that they can read. A class that appears only as a picture of a stamp on a scanned page is invisible to those tools. So a modern program uses both a visible marking for people and a label in the metadata for machines.

Good practice is to mark public items too. Then a missing mark stands out as a mistake. If you find an item with no mark, treat it as the highest class until the owner confirms what it is.

Here is a workplace example. A staff member finds an unmarked folder in a meeting room. He does not assume that it is harmless. He hands it to the proper person, and the owner works out what it is.

Here is your takeaway. Marking is for people, labels are for machines, mark everything including public items, and treat anything unmarked as the highest class.

studyNotes.heading: Safe storage
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at how to store sensitive items, both on paper and in digital form.

Storage rules cover both the physical place and the digital protection. The common controls are these.

- Keep sensitive items in locked rooms, cabinets or safes.
- Allow access only to people with a need to know, which means their job requires it.
- Use encryption, so that a stolen item cannot be read.
- Protect backups as strongly as the live data.
- Protect media from heat, damp and magnetic fields, so that it can still be read later.

Think about how you keep your valuables at home. You put jewelry in a locked box. You do not leave the key sitting on top of the box. And you do not keep your only family photographs in a damp garage.

That image gives us the three ideas that the exam likes.

The first idea is that locks work in layers. A locked cabinet inside a locked room inside a guarded building is harder to defeat than any one of them alone. This is called defense in depth.

The second idea is about keys. Keep encryption keys apart from the data they protect. Leaving them together is like taping your house key to your front door. If a thief carries off the cabinet with the disks and the keys inside it, the encryption has given you nothing.

The third idea is that storage is also about availability. Availability means that the information is there when you need it. Tapes kept in a hot, damp shed may be unreadable when you need them. If the law says that a record must be kept for ten years, you must still be able to read it after ten years. So keep media in a controlled environment, and test-read a sample from time to time.

Here is a workplace example. A bank encrypts its backup disks, keeps them in a fireproof safe in a separate building, keeps the keys under a different person's control, and tests a restore every three months.

Here is what to take away. Lock it up in layers, keep the keys apart from the data, and make sure you can still read it years from now.

studyNotes.heading: Safe transport
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at what happens when information has to move, because this is when it is at extra risk.

Think about moving house with something precious. You pack it carefully, and you may carry it yourself. If you must use a delivery company, you choose one you trust, you get a receipt, and you check the seal when it arrives.

The common controls for moving information follow the same logic.

- Encrypt it before it leaves.
- Use an approved, trusted courier.
- Use tamper-evident packaging, which shows clearly if someone has opened it.
- Keep a chain of custody, which is a signed record of who held the item, when and why.

Encryption is the most important of these, because it protects the information even when everything else goes wrong. If a box of encrypted tapes falls off a van, you have lost some tapes. You have not lost the data.

Chain of custody answers one simple question. Who had it, at every moment? Each person signs when they receive the item and when they pass it on. If a record has a gap, nobody can say what happened during that gap.

Now here is a detail that catches people out. For highly sensitive items, the outer wrapping often carries no class marking. A marking on the outside tells a thief which parcel to steal. The class is shown on an inner wrapping instead. So this is one place where we deliberately do not advertise the class to the world.

Information also moves electronically, and the same thinking applies. Use an approved encrypted service. Make sure that the person receiving it has to prove who they are. Do not put a password in the same email as the file it protects. That is just the house key taped to the door again.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital sends old disks for destruction. They are encrypted, packed in sealed crates, collected by an approved company, and signed for at the hospital and at the destruction site. The record has no gaps.

Here is your takeaway. Encrypt it, seal it, sign for it at every handover, and keep the class off the outer wrapping.

studyNotes.heading: Handling during daily use
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at the moments when information is simply being used, because most mistakes happen during ordinary work.

Think about reading a private letter on a crowded bus. Nothing has been stolen and nobody has broken in, but the person beside you can read every word. Daily use is like that. The threat is usually a careless moment, and not a clever attacker.

Here are the common situations and the sensible rules.

Printing is the first. Sensitive pages left in a printer tray can be read by anyone who walks past. A good fix is to hold each print job until the person who sent it shows a staff badge at the printer. Reminding staff is weaker, because it relies on memory.

Screens are the second. Use automatic screen locks, and privacy filters in public areas. A privacy filter is a thin sheet that makes a screen unreadable from the side.

Desks are the third. A clean desk policy says that sensitive papers are locked away whenever you leave your desk.

Copying is the fourth. Every copy increases the risk and needs the same protection. Handling rules may limit copying for the highest class, and they may require a record of each copy.

Sharing is the fifth. Before information goes to a supplier or partner, the handling rules should travel with it, usually through a contract. An outside party that receives your data must protect it to the agreed level.

Disposal is the last. Each class has its own rule for the end of an item's life. Paper may go through a cross-cut shredder, which cuts in two directions so that strips cannot be rejoined. We will study the methods for electronic media in a later topic.

Here is a workplace example. An insurance office has shared printers, and an auditor finds claims forms left in the trays. The manager does not simply send out a reminder. She turns on badge release at the printer, so the page does not appear until the sender is standing there.

Here is what to take away. Most handling failures are small daily habits, so build the safe behavior into the process and do not rely on people remembering.

studyNotes.heading: A worked example and the downgrade trap
studyNotes.body:
In this final part we will put all of this together with one example, and then look at the trap that the exam most likes to set.

A bank has a printed loan report, classed as Confidential. Let us follow it through its handling rules.

- Marking: Confidential appears at the top and bottom of every page.
- Storage: it stays in a locked cabinet in a restricted room.
- Transport: it goes in a sealed tamper-evident envelope by approved courier, with a signature at each handover.
- Disposal: it goes through a cross-cut shredder, never the normal bin.

Now suppose that a manager needs a copy for a branch in another city. The copy gets the same marking and the same protection. If a scanned version goes by email, the file gets a label in its metadata, it is encrypted, and only the named person can open it. The format has changed, but the rules have not.

Now for the trap. Staff are sometimes tempted to mark an item lower so that it is easier to send. Imagine a parent writing the word cheap on a valuable parcel to save on insurance. The parcel is still valuable, and the risk has not changed.

Only the owner may change a class, and convenience is not a reason to change it. If the secure method is slow, the answer is to use it anyway, or to ask the owner whether the information really is still at that level. A good adviser may also suggest improving the secure method, so that staff are not tempted next time.

If something goes wrong, handling rules connect to incident response. A lost envelope or a misdirected email should be reported at once. Early reporting matters far more than blame. A person who fears punishment hides the mistake, and then nobody can reduce the harm.

Think like a manager. Ask whether the rule is written, whether people know it, whether the secure way is workable, and whether the owner made the decision.

Here is your takeaway. The rules follow the class through every format, only the owner changes a class, and a deadline never does.

keyTerms.meaning: Written rules on how to treat an item of each class throughout its life.
Showing the class of an item in a form people can read, such as a stamp or banner.
A tag showing the class. In exact usage, often a tag inside a system that computers can read.
A person may see information only if their job truly requires it.
Scrambling data so that only someone with the key can read it.
A signed record of who held an item, when and why.
Packaging that shows clearly if someone has opened it.

keyPoints: Handling rules are written per class and cover the item's whole life.
Copies and backups need the same protection as the original.
Treat an unmarked item as the highest class until the owner confirms it.
Encrypt and track sensitive items while they are moving.
Only the owner may change an item's class.
topics.memoryHook: Think of cash at a bank: Mark the bag, Store it in the vault, Move it with signatures.

question.prompt: A law firm sends backup tapes of client files to a storage site each week by courier. Last month a box went missing for several hours before it was found. Which action would BEST protect the client files on future trips?
options: Print CONFIDENTIAL in large letters on the outside of each box so that couriers take extra care
Run backups once a month instead of weekly so that fewer boxes are on the road at any time
Ask a partner of the firm to drive the tapes to the site in a private car
Encrypt the tapes before they leave and log each handover
question.explanation: Encryption keeps the files unreadable if a box is lost, and a custody log shows who held it. Outside markings are tempting, but they tell a thief which box is valuable. Fewer trips or a private car still leave readable files at risk.

practiceQuestions.prompt: To save time, a manager proposes that staff stop marking Public documents and mark only the sensitive ones. What is the BEST advice from the security adviser?
options: Agree, because Public documents carry no risk of any kind and need no handling rules at all
Agree, and ask staff to store all of the unmarked documents together in one shared folder
Disagree, and require every Public document to be encrypted in the same way as sensitive ones
Disagree, because when every item carries a mark, a missing mark stands out as a mistake
practiceQuestions.explanation: When everything carries a mark, an unmarked item is clearly a mistake and can be treated with caution. Agreeing is tempting because Public items need little care, but then nobody can tell a harmless blank from a sensitive item that was never marked.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company stamps its class in large text on the first page of each scanned document. Its new monitoring software, which should act automatically on the class, cannot tell which files are sensitive. What would BEST solve this?
options: Add a machine-readable label to the metadata of each file that can be read by the software
Make the printed stamp larger, and place it in a bolder color on every page of the document
Ask staff to read each file and to tell the monitoring team when a sensitive one is being sent
Stop using the monitoring software and rely on the printed stamp as the only form of marking
practiceQuestions.explanation: A stamp is for people, and automated tools need a label they can read in the file's details. A bigger stamp is tempting, but a picture on a page is still invisible to the software. Relying on staff to report each file does not scale.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company encrypts its archive disks before placing them in a fireproof cabinet. An auditor notices that the printed encryption keys are in an envelope inside the same cabinet. What is the BEST corrective action?
options: Buy a second, stronger fireproof cabinet, and keep both the disks and the keys inside that one
Seal the envelope with tamper-evident tape and then leave it where it is in the cabinet
Store the keys separately from the disks, under the control of a different authorized person
Encrypt the disks a second time using a longer key, and leave the rest of the process unchanged
practiceQuestions.explanation: Anyone who takes the cabinet's contents gets both the disks and the means to read them, so the keys must be kept apart. Tamper-evident tape is tempting, but it only shows that someone opened the envelope after the harm is done.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A customer database sits in a locked, monitored data center and is encrypted. Its nightly backup disks, which hold the same data, are unencrypted on an open shelf in the IT (information technology) office. What is the BEST recommendation?
options: Make backups less often, so that fewer disks are sitting on the shelf at any one time
Give the backup disks the same protection that the original database already has
Put a sign on the shelf telling all staff and visitors that the backup disks are confidential
Leave the disks there, since the live database is the one that attackers would want to reach
practiceQuestions.explanation: A backup holds the same information, so it needs the same protection. Making backups less often is tempting because it reduces the number of disks, but the remaining disks are still exposed and recovery becomes worse.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A hospital sends old drives to a destruction company. During an audit, it cannot show who held the drives between its loading dock and the destruction site. Which control was MOST clearly missing?
options: A class marking on the outside of every shipping crate
A review of the destruction company's financial accounts
An extra overwrite of each drive before it left the building
A signed chain of custody record at every handover point
practiceQuestions.explanation: A chain of custody records who held an item, when and why, which is precisely what the hospital cannot show. An extra overwrite is tempting because it reduces the data at risk, but it would not answer who held the drives.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An agency must send a highly classified paper document by approved courier. Which packaging approach is BEST?
options: One envelope with the class printed clearly on the outside, so that the courier knows to take special care
One plain envelope with the class marked nowhere at all, including on the document inside it
A plain outer wrapping with no class shown, and the class marked on an inner wrapping
A clear plastic bag, so the courier can see at a glance that the document is still inside it
practiceQuestions.explanation: The plain outer layer does not tell a thief what is valuable, and the inner wrapping tells the authorized receiver how to treat it. Printing the class outside is tempting because it seems to encourage care, but it advertises the target.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Sensitive reports are often left in the tray of a shared office printer for hours. Staff say that they simply forget to collect them. What would BEST address the cause?
options: Hold each print job on the system until the person who sent it badges in at the printer
Send a reminder email each month asking all staff to collect their printing more quickly
Move the printer into the manager's office so that the manager can watch what is printed on it
Empty the tray at the end of each day and put whatever is found into the ordinary waste bin
practiceQuestions.explanation: Holding the job until the person is standing at the printer removes the dependence on memory. A reminder is tempting because it is cheap, but staff have already said that forgetting is the problem. Ordinary waste bins would create a new exposure.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Three departments handle the same class of report in three different ways. One emails it openly, one encrypts it, and one will only hand over paper. Staff say that nobody has told them the rules. What is the BEST action?
options: Choose the strictest department and tell the other two departments to copy it without any written rules
Buy an email encryption product and install it for all of the staff in those three departments
Ask each of the three department heads to write their own handling rules for their own staff
Publish written handling rules for each class, and then train the staff in all departments
practiceQuestions.explanation: The cause is that no shared written rule exists and nobody has been trained on one. Buying encryption is tempting, but a tool cannot fix a missing rule. Separate department rules would keep the inconsistency.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company must be able to read its archive tapes for ten years. The tapes are currently stored in a hot, damp shed beside a large electric motor. What is the BEST recommendation?
options: Move the tapes into the main office, and ask the staff to keep a close eye on them during the day
Store them in a controlled environment, and test-read a sample of the tapes from time to time
Keep them in the shed, but wrap each tape in plastic and label it carefully with the current year
Make a second copy and store it in the same shed so that there is always one spare tape available
practiceQuestions.explanation: Heat, damp and magnetic fields can make media unreadable, and only testing proves that it can still be read. A second copy is tempting, but a copy in the same shed suffers from the same conditions.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An accountant must send a Confidential file to an outside auditor today. Which method BEST meets typical handling rules for that class?
options: Email the file in a password-protected archive and put the password in the same email message
Upload the file to a personal online storage account, then share a public link with the auditor
Use the approved encrypted transfer service, and require the auditor to sign in to collect it
Change the class to Public, email the file, then change the class back once it has been received
practiceQuestions.explanation: An approved encrypted service protects the file on its way and proves who collects it. The password-protected archive is tempting because it looks like encryption, but the password travels with the file, so anyone who gets the email can open it.

topics.name: Provision information and assets securely: ownership, inventory, asset management
topics.simpleExplanation: To provision means to supply something to someone. When a shop gives a new worker keys and a uniform, it writes that down, and it gets them back when the worker leaves. Organizations must do the same with laptops, software and access to information. Every item needs a named owner. Every item goes on a list, called an inventory. Asset management is the ongoing work of tracking each item from the day it arrives until the day it is retired.

studyNotes.heading: Provisioning securely
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at what it means to provision something securely, which is the first idea in this objective.

To provision means to supply. Secure provisioning means giving people the information and equipment they need in a controlled way, and nothing extra. Two ideas guide it.

- Need to know: you see information only if your job requires it.
- Least privilege: you get the smallest set of rights that lets you do your job.

These two sound alike, but they answer different questions. Need to know is about which information you may see. Least privilege is about what you may do, such as read, change or delete.

Think about a babysitter. You give the babysitter the front door key. You do not hand over the key to your safe, or your bank card. The babysitter gets what the job needs, and you take the key back at the end of the evening.

Now think about a workplace. A new payroll clerk needs to read and enter pay details. The clerk does not need to change the structure of the payroll database. And the clerk does not need the records of the board of directors.

The business owner of the information approves access. The technical team carries out the decision. The person asking for access should not be the person approving it. Keeping those jobs apart is called separation of duties. It means that no single person can complete a sensitive task alone.

A common shortcut causes real harm. The help desk sets up a new person by copying a colleague's rights. Those rights may be years out of date and far too wide. A better way is to give rights according to a defined role, which has been approved in advance.

Provisioning also needs a way back. When someone changes jobs or leaves, the organization must remove rights and collect equipment. People who move jobs and keep their old rights slowly collect far more access than they need. This is called privilege creep. Regular access reviews catch it.

Here is what to take away. Give only what the job needs, have the owner approve it, and take it back when the job changes.

studyNotes.heading: Ownership and accountability
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at ownership, because the exam treats it as the foundation of everything else in this domain.

Every asset needs a named owner. An asset is anything of value, such as information, a system or a piece of equipment. The owner is a person with authority in the business, and the owner answers for how the asset is protected.

An owner may hand out the daily work. An owner cannot hand away the accountability. Think of a landlord who hires a cleaner. The cleaner does the work, but the landlord still answers for the building. If a tenant is hurt on a wet floor, nobody is going to accept that the landlord had forgotten about it.

The exam uses two words with care. Accountable means that you answer for the result. Responsible means that you carry out the task. You can share responsibility among many people. Accountability stays with one named person.

What does an owner actually do? The owner decides the class of the information. The owner approves who may have access. The owner agrees the level of protection, and accepts the risk that is left over. The owner also makes sure that access is reviewed.

Here is a workplace example. The finance director owns the payroll data. She asks an assistant to carry out the quarterly access reviews. The assistant forgets for six months. The assistant failed in a task, but the finance director is still accountable for the fact that it did not happen.

The owner should be a business person, and not simply someone from the technical team. The business knows what the information is worth and what it is used for. A system owner, by contrast, answers for a particular system, such as the payroll application, and for making sure that it is protected. In a small company, one person may hold both roles.

An asset with no owner is an asset nobody protects. Nobody approves its access, nobody budgets for it, and nobody notices when it is out of date. When you find such an asset, your first job is to find out who uses it, and to have management name an owner.

Here is your takeaway. Owners can delegate the work, but they keep the accountability.

studyNotes.heading: The inventory: tangible assets
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will begin looking at the inventory, and we will start with the things that you can touch.

An inventory is a complete, current list of what the organization has. The outline splits assets into two kinds, tangible and intangible. Tangible assets can be touched. They include laptops, servers, phones, network equipment, paper records and buildings. A server is a central computer that serves many users.

Think about the home insurance form that asks what you own. If your television is stolen and you have no idea of the make, the model or when you bought it, you will struggle to claim. You must know what you have before you can protect it or replace it.

A useful inventory record shows what the item is, who owns it, where it is, its class and its current state. For a laptop, that may include the serial number, the person it was issued to, the software on it, and whether it is in use, in repair or retired.

Here is why this matters for security. The inventory supports nearly everything else.

You need it to assess risk, because you cannot weigh the risk to something you have forgotten. You need it to find what must be patched, which means fixed with an update from the maker. You need it to learn what was affected during an incident. And you need it when you retire equipment, so that nothing leaves the building with data still on it.

Here is a workplace example. A police station keeps a register of its radios and laptops. Each item has an asset tag, which is a numbered label, and each one is signed out to a named officer. When a radio goes missing, the register shows who last held it and which channels it could reach, so the right people are told and the radio can be locked out.

Inventories go stale quickly. A list that was correct in January may be badly wrong by July. So the inventory must be kept current as a normal part of work, and not rebuilt in a rush for each audit.

Here is what to take away. Record what it is, who owns it, where it is and what class it is, and keep that record current.

studyNotes.heading: The inventory: intangible assets
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the other half of the inventory, the things you cannot touch, which are the ones that people most often forget.

Intangible assets cannot be touched. They include data, software licenses, patents, trademarks, brand and reputation. A patent is a legal right over an invention. A trademark is a protected name or symbol.

Think about a small family bakery. The ovens are tangible. But the secret recipe, the name that the town knows and trusts, and the list of regular customers are all intangible. If the ovens break, you can buy new ones. If the recipe leaks or the name is ruined, you may not recover. Intangible assets are frequently worth more than the physical ones.

Four kinds of intangible asset are worth thinking about at work.

Data comes first. It belongs in the inventory like anything else, with its owner, class and location.

Software and licenses come next. A license is the legal permission to use a product. If a company is using 500 copies but holds licenses for only 300, it is 200 short. That is a legal and financial risk, and it is the kind of problem that a software inventory exposes.

A related idea is the software bill of materials, or SBOM. It is a list of the components inside a software product, much like the list of ingredients on a food packet. When a flaw is announced in a popular component, the list tells you where that component is.

Then comes intellectual property, meaning creations of the mind that have value, such as designs, trade secrets, patents and trademarks. A trade secret is protected only as long as it stays secret, so handling rules matter a great deal.

Last come brand and reputation. You cannot list them with a serial number, but they belong in risk discussions, because a breach can damage them for years.

Here is a workplace example. A company's register lists every laptop and phone, and nothing else. A manager points out that its customer data, its licenses and its product designs are worth many times more than the hardware, and none of them are listed.

Here is your takeaway. An inventory that only counts hardware is only half an inventory.

studyNotes.heading: Finding what is really out there
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at how to check the inventory against reality, and what to do when the two do not agree.

Think about checking your kitchen cupboards against your shopping list. The list says that you have rice. The cupboard says that you do not. And there is a jar at the back that you have never seen before. The difference between the list and the shelf is the part that deserves your attention.

Automated discovery tools do this job for an organization. They scan the network and report on what they find. The team compares what they find with the list, and then investigates any difference.

There are two kinds of difference. An item may be on the list but not found. It could be lost, stolen, switched off, or sitting in a drawer. Or an item may be found but not on the list. It may be a personal device, a forgotten old server, or even an intruder's equipment.

The right first step in both cases is to investigate. Do not delete the results. Do not add the unknown items to the list just to make the numbers match. And do not rip everything off the network without knowing what it does, because it may be supporting something important.

An item found on the network but missing from the list may be shadow IT. That means technology that staff use without approval from the information technology, or IT, team. Cloud services, which are computing bought online from another company, make this easy, because anyone with a payment card can start one.

Shadow IT usually means that staff have a real need that is not being met. So a wise manager does two things. The manager brings the service under control, with a named owner and a place in the inventory. And the manager asks why people felt that they had to go around the approved route.

Here is a workplace example. A marketing team has started using an online design tool, and has uploaded a customer list to it. The security manager records the tool, finds an owner, checks the contract and moves the customer list to an approved place.

Here is what to take away. Compare the list with reality, investigate every difference, and deal with the cause of shadow IT.

studyNotes.heading: Asset management and a worked example
studyNotes.body:
In this final part we will look at asset management as a whole, and we will follow one laptop from the day it was requested to the day it comes back.

Asset management is the ongoing process of tracking each asset through its whole life. A common order is: request, approve, buy, record, configure, issue, maintain, retire, and dispose. Many organizations keep this in a configuration management database, or CMDB, a central record of assets and how they are set up.

Think about a library book. It is bought, it is catalogued, it is lent, it is returned, it is repaired, and one day it is withdrawn. At any moment the library can tell you where it is.

Here is the worked example. A new bank teller needs a laptop.

- Step 1: The teller's manager requests it.
- Step 2: The owner approves access to the account system.
- Step 3: The IT team, meaning information technology, records the laptop's serial number in the inventory.
- Step 4: IT sets it up to the secure standard, with only the needed software.
- Step 5: The teller signs for it.
- Step 6: Access is reviewed each year.
- Step 7: On leaving, rights are removed and the laptop is returned and checked off.

Notice that the steps depend on each other, and that the leaving step depends on someone telling IT. If human resources does not tell IT that a person has left, the laptop and the access both go on existing. The proper fix is to link the leaving process to asset return and access removal.

The same is true of changes. If a system is changed but nobody updates the record, then the record is wrong when it matters most, in the middle of an incident. The fix is to make the update a required step of change management, which is the controlled process for approving and recording changes.

Think like a manager. If an audit finds items missing, the fix is a better process, not simply buying replacements.

Here is your takeaway. Track every asset from request to disposal, and fix the process whenever the record and reality drift apart.

keyTerms.meaning: Supplying information, equipment or access to someone in a controlled way.
The person with business authority who answers for an asset and its protection.
A complete, current list of the organization's assets.
An asset you can touch, such as a laptop or a building.
An asset you cannot touch, such as data, a patent or a good reputation.
Giving a person only the smallest set of rights needed for the job.
Technology that staff use without approval from the information technology team.
Configuration Management Database: a central record of assets and how they are set up.

keyPoints: Every asset needs a named owner who stays accountable.
The inventory must cover both tangible and intangible assets.
Give only what the job needs, and take it back when the job changes.
Compare discovery scans with the inventory and investigate any difference.
An accurate inventory supports risk work, patching and incident response.
topics.memoryHook: Keys and uniform: sign them out, write them down, get them back.

question.prompt: A school's security manager learns that several departments have signed up for online file-sharing services without telling the IT (information technology) team. Student records may be stored in them. What is the BEST next step?
options: Find these services, record them in the inventory, and give each one an owner
Block all internet access from school computers until a full investigation has been carried out
Tell the departments to stop and delete their accounts at once, without keeping any record of them
Buy a larger approved file server so that staff will have no reason to look elsewhere
question.explanation: You must first know what exists and who answers for it, and then decisions can follow. Deleting accounts at once is tempting, but it could lose student records and it hides the size of the problem. Blocking everything stops the school working, and a bigger server does not deal with the records already out there.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A developer emails the database team asking for access to the live payroll database. An administrator grants it, because the developer seems to have a good reason. What was the MAIN failure?
options: The developer should have asked in person rather than by sending an email to the database team
The administrator should have waited until the next planned maintenance window to grant the access
The data owner did not approve the access before the administrator granted it
The access should have been granted only after the developer had finished security awareness training
practiceQuestions.explanation: The business owner approves access, and the technical team carries the decision out. Waiting for a maintenance window is tempting because it sounds like good process, but timing does not fix the fact that the wrong person made the decision.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Over eight years, an employee has worked in four departments. A review shows that she still has access rights from all four jobs. Which control would BEST prevent this from happening again?
options: Remove the old rights at each job change, and review everyone's access on a regular schedule
Require her and all other long-serving staff to change their passwords more often than others
Give her a new account at each job change, and leave the old accounts in place in case they are needed
Record every action that long-serving staff take and keep those records for seven years
practiceQuestions.explanation: This is privilege creep, and it is stopped by removing rights when a job changes and by regular reviews to catch what is missed. Recording actions is tempting because it creates evidence, but the excess access would remain.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The finance director owns the company's payroll data. She asks an assistant to carry out the quarterly access reviews. The assistant misses two reviews, and an auditor reports the gap. Who is accountable for the missed reviews?
options: The assistant, because accountability moved when the task was handed over
The finance director, because owners cannot delegate accountability for their data
The auditor, because the auditor did not report the missing reviews sooner
The IT (information technology) team, because the access rights are held on its systems
practiceQuestions.explanation: An owner may hand over the work but keeps the accountability. The assistant is tempting, since the assistant did fail in a task, but that is responsibility for the task and not accountability for the result.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's asset register lists every laptop, server and phone, and nothing else. The security manager is asked what the register is MOST seriously missing. Which answer is BEST?
options: Furniture and other office items that are physically present in each of the buildings
A column giving the color and the weight of each laptop, server and telephone in the list
The personal phones and home computers of each member of staff and of their families
Intangible assets, such as the company's data, its software licenses and its patents
practiceQuestions.explanation: An inventory should cover tangible and intangible assets, and intangible ones are often worth the most. Furniture is tempting because it is an asset too, but it adds little to security compared with data, licenses and patents.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An automated network scan finds 14 devices that do not appear in the inventory. What should the security team do FIRST?
options: Investigate each one to learn what the device is, what it does and who is responsible for it
Disconnect all 14 devices from the network at once and then destroy them as unknown equipment
Add all 14 devices to the inventory with no further checks, so that the two lists will agree
Delete the scan results, because the inventory is the approved record and takes priority
practiceQuestions.explanation: Every difference must be understood before anyone acts. Disconnecting at once is tempting because unknown devices are worrying, but one of them may support something important, and destroying them would also destroy evidence.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Several departing staff have left without returning their laptops. Each time, the IT (information technology) team learns of the departure weeks later. What would BEST fix the cause?
options: Buy laptops at a cheaper price so that each one lost costs the company rather less money
Send a stronger letter reminding former staff that laptops belong to the company
Link the human resources leaving process to equipment return and to access removal
Ask line managers to keep a spreadsheet of laptops that they think are in their own teams
practiceQuestions.explanation: The cause is that the leaving process does not tell the people who collect equipment and remove access. A stronger letter is tempting, but it comes after the laptop has already gone, and it does nothing about the access that remained.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During an audit, a server is found that runs an old application. Nobody claims it, no budget covers it, and it has not been updated for years. What is the BEST next step?
options: Switch it off right away and wipe its disks, because nobody has come forward to claim it
Leave it running untouched, because changing it could harm a process that nobody knows about
Ask the newest member of the IT (information technology) team to look after it from now on
Find out who uses the server in the business, and have management name an owner for it
practiceQuestions.explanation: Without an owner, nobody can decide on its protection, its budget or its future. Wiping it is tempting because it looks like an easy way to remove the risk, but it could stop a real business process and destroy needed data.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A software maker's audit finds that a company is using 500 copies of a product but holds licenses for only 300. Staff installed the extra copies over time, and nobody kept count. Which action would BEST prevent this from happening again?
options: Buy an additional 1,000 licenses so that the company will always have far more than it needs
Track all software and its licenses as assets in the inventory, and keep the count current
Ban all software purchases across the company until the next audit has been carried out
Uninstall the product from every computer and ask staff to find a free alternative product
practiceQuestions.explanation: Licenses are intangible assets, and tracking them is what prevents the count from drifting. Buying a large surplus is tempting because it removes the shortage for now, but it wastes money and nobody would still be counting.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During an incident, responders relied on the configuration management database, a central record of assets and how they are set up. It was wrong, because recent changes were never recorded. What is the BEST corrective action?
options: Stop using the database, and ask staff to keep their own personal notes about every system
Rebuild the database by hand once every year and keep the rest of the process just as it is
Make updating the record a required step of the change management process for every system
Buy a second database and keep a copy there so that the responders have two records to compare
practiceQuestions.explanation: The cause is that changes do not update the record, so the update must become part of the change process. A yearly rebuild is tempting because it does correct the data, but the record would drift again the next day.

practiceQuestions.prompt: To save time, the help desk sets up each new employee by copying the access rights of a colleague in the same team. What is the BEST replacement for this practice?
options: Grant only the rights that have been approved in advance for the person's defined role
Copy the rights from the most senior person on the team, so that nobody ever lacks any access
Give each new employee full access for thirty days and then remove whatever was not used by them
Keep copying rights, and ask each new employee to tell the help desk about any they do not need
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rights based on an approved role follow least privilege and do not inherit a colleague's old access. Asking new staff to report extra rights is tempting because it seems to involve them, but they cannot know what they should not have.

topics.name: Data lifecycle and data roles: owners, controllers, custodians, processors, users, subjects; collection, location, maintenance
topics.simpleExplanation: Data has a life, a bit like a library book. It arrives, it is stored, people use it, and one day it leaves. At each stage, somebody has a job to do. One person decides the rules. Another looks after the data every day. Others just use it. And the data may be about a real person, who has rights. The exam expects you to know each role exactly. You must also know what to collect, where to keep it, and how to maintain it.

studyNotes.heading: The data lifecycle
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at the life of a piece of data, from the moment it appears until the moment it is gone.

A lifecycle is the set of stages something goes through. A common model for data has six stages, in this order.

- Create or collect
- Store
- Use
- Share
- Archive
- Destroy

To archive means to move data to long-term storage, because it is no longer in daily use but must still be kept.

Think about a library book. It arrives and is catalogued. It is put on a shelf. People read it in the building. It is lent to someone else. When it is rarely wanted, it moves to a store room. And one day it is withdrawn and pulped. At every stage, the library knows what should happen to it.

Now let us follow something real. A job applicant fills in an online form. That is the create or collect stage. The form is saved to a database. That is store. A recruiter reads it. That is use. The recruiter sends it to the hiring manager. That is share. After the post is filled, the record moves to cheaper storage for the period the law requires. That is archive. When that period ends, the record is securely removed. That is destroy.

Three ideas apply across the whole cycle.

The first is that security applies at every stage. Many organizations protect the store stage very well, and then forget about the copies shared by email.

The second is that the class follows the data from start to finish. An archived record is not less sensitive just because nobody is looking at it. The class should be decided as early as possible, ideally when the data is created or collected, so that the right rules apply from the first day.

The third is that different people have different duties at each stage. That brings us to the roles, which the exam tests very closely.

Here is what to take away. Create or collect, store, use, share, archive, destroy. The class travels with the data all the way through, and nothing is finished until the data has been properly destroyed.

studyNotes.heading: Inside the organization: owner, custodian and user
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at the three data roles found inside an organization. These are the owner, the custodian and the user.

Think about leaving your car with a hotel parking attendant. You own the car, and you decide who may drive it. The attendant parks it, keeps it safe and hands it back, following your wishes. The attendant does not decide to lend it to a friend. Your passenger simply rides in it, and must behave.

The data owner is a senior manager who is accountable for the data. The owner sets its class, decides who may access it, and decides how much protection it needs. The owner usually comes from the business side. The head of sales would own customer sales data, for example.

The data custodian is usually technical staff. The custodian does the daily care the owner asks for, such as making backups, applying security settings and restoring data when needed. The custodian does not decide what the class is, or who should get access. The custodian carries out those decisions.

The data user is anyone who uses the data for their job and must follow the rules. Users only use data for the approved purpose. Users also report anything that looks wrong.

The key sentence for the exam is this. The owner is accountable, and the custodian is responsible for doing the work. Accountable means that you answer for the result. Responsible means that you carry out the task.

Here is a workplace example. In a bank, the head of lending owns the loan records and decides that loan officers may read them. A database administrator is the custodian, and sets up the permissions and runs the backups. A loan officer is the user, and looks up a customer's loan.

If a question asks who decides, look for the owner. If it asks who runs the backups, look for the custodian.

You may also meet the words data steward and system owner. A steward looks after the quality and meaning of data on behalf of the business. A system owner answers for a particular system. Neither replaces the data owner.

Here is your takeaway. The owner decides and is accountable, the custodian carries it out, and the user follows the rules.

studyNotes.heading: Privacy roles: controller, processor and subject
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at three roles that come from privacy law, and then we will place all six roles in one example.

These terms are strongly linked to the General Data Protection Regulation, or GDPR, the European Union privacy law. Personal data means any information about an identifiable living person.

The data controller is the person or organization that decides why personal data is used and how. In practice, it is usually the organization, not one employee. Two organizations that decide together are joint controllers.

The data processor is a separate party that handles personal data for the controller and follows the controller's instructions. The word separate matters. A company's own IT department, meaning its information technology staff, is not a processor. It is part of the controller, and it acts as a custodian.

The data subject is the living person the personal data is about. Subjects have rights, including the right to see their data, to have errors corrected, and in some cases to have it erased. The controller must see that those rights are met.

Think about a dry cleaner. You decide that your suit needs cleaning, and why. The dry cleaner does the work on your instructions. If the dry cleaner starts wearing your suit to parties, it has stopped following instructions. In the same way, a processor that decides for itself why and how data is used is treated as a controller for that use.

Under GDPR, hiring a processor does not end the controller's accountability. The processor has its own legal duties too. There must be a written contract. A processor needs the controller's permission to use another processor. If a processor has a breach, it must tell the controller without undue delay. The controller must normally tell the regulator within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, where that is feasible.

Here is a worked example. A shop runs a loyalty card scheme.

- The shop is the controller.
- The marketing director is the data owner.
- The database team is the custodian.
- An outside mailing company is the processor.
- The cashier who looks up points is a user.
- The customer with the card is the subject.

Here is what to take away. The controller decides why and how, the processor follows instructions, and accountability stays with the controller.

studyNotes.heading: Data collection
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the first stage of the lifecycle more closely, which is deciding what to collect in the first place.

Collect only what you really need for a stated purpose. This is called data minimization. Data you never collected cannot be stolen from you.

Think about someone at your front door asking to read the meter. You show them the meter. You do not also hand them your bank statements. They have no reason to see those, and the more you give out, the more can go wrong.

A school needs a parent's phone number. It does not need the parent's salary. Four ideas should guide every collection.

The first idea is notice. People should be told what is being collected, why it is being collected, and who will receive it.

The second idea is lawful basis. There must be a lawful reason to collect personal data. Under the General Data Protection Regulation, or GDPR, the European Union privacy law, consent is only one possible basis. Others include carrying out a contract and meeting a legal duty.

The third idea is purpose limitation. Do not quietly use data for a new purpose later. If phone numbers were collected to arrange deliveries, then sending sales messages to them is a new purpose, and it needs its own lawful basis.

The fourth idea is quality. Data should be accurate and relevant when it is collected, because every later decision depends on it.

Here is a workplace example. A gym's sign-up form asks for name, phone number, date of birth, salary and employer. The gym uses only the first three.
