The right action is to remove the last two questions. Making them optional does not solve the problem, because the gym would still be holding data that it has no use for. And encrypting those answers would be protecting something that should not exist.

Collection also has a security side. Forms must send data safely, input should be checked, and a class should be assigned to the data as soon as it arrives.

Think like an adviser. The cheapest and strongest control for unneeded data is not to have it.

Here is your takeaway. Collect the minimum, tell people why, have a lawful basis, and keep to the stated purpose.

studyNotes.heading: Data location
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at where data is kept, and why the answer can be a legal question as well as a technical one.

Think about taking something across a national border. The moment you cross, a different set of laws applies to you and to what you are carrying. Data is much the same.

The laws of a country can apply to data stored there. Data sovereignty is the idea that data is subject to the laws of the place where it is held. Data residency means an organization or a law requires the data to stay in a certain place. Some countries go further and pass data localization laws, which require certain data to be stored or processed inside the country.

So sovereignty is about whose law applies. Residency is about where the data must sit.

A court in the country where your data is held may be able to order its disclosure, whatever your home country thinks about that. That is a real risk, and it belongs in the decision about where to store data.

The cloud, which means computers run by another company, makes this harder. You may choose one region for your data, while the provider's default setting copies backups to another continent. So before moving data to the cloud, check which countries will hold it, including backups, logs and support staff access. Support staff in another country who can read the data may count as a transfer.

Personal data leaving the European Union needs a legal route under the General Data Protection Regulation, or GDPR. Examples are a formal decision that the other country gives adequate protection, or an approved set of contract terms.

Encryption is a good protection, but it does not cancel these legal rules. Check the law and the contract first, and involve legal advisers.

Here is a workplace example. A bank's contract says that customer data stays in its home country. The cloud provider's main storage is in that country, but its backups are not. The security manager has the backups restricted to in-country locations, and has this written into the contract.

Here is what to take away. Know every place your data sits, including backups, and check the law and contracts before you move it.

studyNotes.heading: Data maintenance
studyNotes.body:
In this final part we will look at what happens during the long middle of the lifecycle, when data simply has to be looked after.

Maintenance means keeping data correct, useful and safe while you hold it. It is like looking after a house. Nothing dramatic happens most days. But if you stop checking the roof and the pipes, you find out about it at the worst possible moment.

Maintenance includes these jobs.

- Correcting errors and keeping records up to date.
- Making and testing backups.
- Reviewing who has access.
- Applying updates to the systems that hold the data.
- Checking that the class is still right.

Let us look at why each one matters.

Correct data is part of integrity, which means keeping data accurate. Under privacy law, people may also have the right to have mistakes corrected. Wrong data can cause real harm. Think of a hospital record with the wrong allergy on it.

Backups are only useful if they work. A backup that has never been restored is a hope and not a plan. So test restores on a regular schedule. A company might run backups every night for three years, and learn only when a disk fails that none of them can be restored.

Access reviews catch people who have changed jobs or left. The owner should confirm that each person still needs access.

Updates, also called patches, fix known weaknesses in the systems that hold data.

Class checks matter because value changes with time, and because new combinations of data can become more sensitive.

Here is a workplace example that brings the roles together. A health insurer's customer data needs yearly care. The data owner confirms the class and signs off the access list. The custodian runs the backups, tests a restore and applies the patches. Users correct errors as they find them. An outside processor follows the insurer's written instructions. The people that the data is about can ask to see it and correct it.

The owner stays accountable for this work, even though the custodian carries it out.

Think like a manager. Maintenance is a routine with named people and dates, and not a task left for when something breaks.

Here is your takeaway. Keep data accurate, test your restores, review access, patch systems, and recheck the class.
