question.prompt: A clinic decides which patient details it collects and why. It pays an outside company to print and post patient letters, and that company works only on the clinic's instructions. The outside company then suffers a data breach. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: The outside company became the controller when it received the data, so the clinic has no further duty
The clinic alone is at fault, because a processor never has any legal duties of its own
The clinic stays accountable as controller, and the company also has duties as processor
The patients are custodians of their own details, so each patient must manage the breach
question.explanation: The clinic decides why and how, so it is the controller and stays accountable. The company follows instructions, so it is the processor, and processors have duties too. It is tempting to think hiring a company passes on the blame, but accountability does not move that way. Patients are data subjects.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A database administrator at a bank runs the backups, applies the security settings and restores data, all according to rules set by the head of lending. Which data role does the administrator hold?
options: Data owner
Data custodian
Data subject
Data controller
practiceQuestions.explanation: The custodian does the daily care that the owner asks for. Data owner is tempting because the administrator has great technical power over the data, but the head of lending sets the rules.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's own IT (information technology) department runs the servers that hold the staff records. The company decides what is collected and why. A consultant describes the department as the company's data processor. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: The consultant is right, because anyone who touches personal data is legally a processor
The department is the controller, because it physically holds all of the staff records
The department is the data subject, because its own staff appear in the records it holds
The department acts as a custodian, because a processor is always a separate party
practiceQuestions.explanation: A processor is a separate party acting for the controller, so an internal department is part of the controller and acts as a custodian. The consultant's view is tempting because the department does handle the data, but handling alone does not make a processor.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A retailer hires a mailing company to send its customer newsletter, under a contract limiting the company to that task. The mailing company secretly uses the customer list to advertise its own services. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: It is still only a processor, because a contract with the retailer exists and has not ended
The customers have become its custodians, because they received its advertising in the post
For that use it has acted as a controller, and it has to answer for that decision
The retailer has become a processor, because the mailing company now makes the decisions
practiceQuestions.explanation: A processor that decides for itself why and how data is used is treated as a controller for that use. The first option is tempting because the contract still exists, but the mailing company went outside it. The retailer does not become a processor.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A customer notices that a shop's records show her old address, and she asks the shop to correct it. The shop decides what customer data is collected and why, and an outside firm hosts the records on the shop's instructions. Who must see that her request is met?
options: The shop, because the controller must see that a data subject's rights are met
The customer, as the data subject, by logging in and fixing the records herself
The outside firm, which must decide by itself whether the request should be met
The cashier who last served her, as the data user who happens to know her address
practiceQuestions.explanation: The controller must see that the subject's rights are met, even if a processor does the technical work. The outside firm is tempting because it holds the records, but a processor acts on instructions and does not decide.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An outside company processes customer data on an insurer's instructions. The company discovers that its system has been breached and the insurer's data exposed. Under the General Data Protection Regulation, which notification duty applies to the company?
options: Contact each affected customer directly and decide the message, without informing the insurer
Wait for the results of a full investigation, which can take several months, and then report
Say nothing, because the duty to report a breach falls only on the controller and never on a processor
Tell the insurer without undue delay, so that the insurer can meet its own duties
practiceQuestions.explanation: A processor must tell its controller without undue delay, and the controller then deals with the regulator, normally within 72 hours of becoming aware. Waiting for a full investigation is tempting because the facts would be clearer, but it would use up the controller's time.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A gym's online sign-up form asks for name, phone number, date of birth, salary and employer. The gym uses only the name, phone number and date of birth. What is the BEST action?
options: Keep the form as it is and encrypt the salary and employer fields in the database
Remove the questions about salary and employer from the form, and stop collecting both
Keep the form as it is and add a line telling members the fields may be useful one day
Make the salary and employer questions optional, and keep all of the answers that are given
practiceQuestions.explanation: Data minimization means collecting only what is needed for a stated purpose. Encryption is tempting because it is a strong control, but the gym should not hold the data at all. Optional questions would still collect data it has no use for.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An online shop collected phone numbers only to arrange deliveries. The marketing team now wants to send sales messages to those numbers. What should the privacy adviser recommend FIRST?
options: Go ahead, because the shop already holds the numbers and they were collected lawfully
Go ahead, but send sales messages only once a month so that customers are not disturbed
Check whether there is a lawful basis for using the numbers for this new purpose
Delete all of the phone numbers, because any thought of new use has already made them unlawful
practiceQuestions.explanation: Purpose limitation means data collected for one purpose cannot simply be reused for another. It is tempting to go ahead because the numbers were lawfully collected, but that lawful reason covered deliveries only.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A contract requires a bank's customer data to stay within its home country. The cloud provider's main storage is in that country, but its default backup setting copies data to another continent. What is the BEST action?
options: Accept the setting, because only the main copy counts for the purposes of this type of contract
Encrypt the backups, as encrypted copies are exempt from any limit on where data may be kept
Stop taking backups altogether, so that no copy of the data can ever leave the home country
Restrict the backups to locations in that country, and confirm this in the contract
practiceQuestions.explanation: Backups are copies of the data, so the residency requirement applies to them as well. Encryption is tempting, but it does not cancel a legal or contract rule about location. Stopping backups would put availability at serious risk.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's legal team warns that because its files are held on servers in a certain foreign country, that country's courts may be able to order their disclosure. Which concept does this warning BEST describe?
options: Data sovereignty
Data minimization
Purpose limitation
Data remanence
practiceQuestions.explanation: Data sovereignty is the idea that data falls under the laws of the place where it is held. Data remanence is tempting because the words sound technical and related, but it means data left behind after an attempt to remove it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has run nightly backups of its customer records for three years. When a disk failed last week, it learned that the backups could not be restored. Which maintenance step would BEST have prevented this?
options: Buying larger backup disks, so that the nightly backup could hold several more years of data
Testing a full restore from those backups on a regular, recorded schedule
Running the backup twice each night and keeping each of the copies on the same backup system
Reviewing who has access to the backup system every three months
practiceQuestions.explanation: Only a test restore proves that backups work. Running two backups a night is tempting because it sounds safer, but two copies made by the same faulty process would both fail. An access review is useful, but it does not prove that restores work.

topics.name: Asset retention and end of life: EOL, EOS, data remanence, destruction methods such as clearing, purging, destroying, degaussing, crypto-erase
topics.simpleExplanation: Nothing should be kept forever. Keep data for as long as the law and the business need it, and then remove it safely. Equipment and software also get old, and makers stop fixing them. Removing data is harder than it sounds. Deleting a file is like tearing the index card out of a library drawer while the book stays on the shelf. Someone can still find it. So we choose a removal method that matches how sensitive the data is.

studyNotes.heading: Retention and legal holds
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at how long information should be kept, and what can interrupt the normal timetable.

Retention means keeping data for a set period. A retention policy lists each type of data and how long to keep it, based on laws, contracts and business need.

Think about the papers in your own home. You keep tax papers for a certain number of years, because you may be asked for them. You keep your birth certificate for life. You throw away last month's flyers. Each kind of paper has its own sensible period.

Keeping data forever feels safe, but it is not. It costs money. It gives thieves more to steal. And it gives the other side in a court case more to ask for. Old data that has no remaining use is all risk and no value. Under many privacy laws, personal data must not be kept longer than it is needed.

There are two ways to get this wrong. Destroying data too early can break the law. Keeping data too long can also break the law. So a retention schedule needs input from legal advisers and from the data owners.

Here is a worked example. Suppose a tax law requires invoices to be kept for seven years. An invoice from March 2020 must be kept until March 2027. After that date, with no other reason to keep it, it should be securely destroyed.

Now for the interruption. A legal hold is an order to keep certain data because of a court case or investigation. It overrides normal deletion until it is lifted. Suppose that the same invoice is part of a dispute, and a lawsuit begins in February 2027. Automatic deletion must be suspended for the relevant data, and the invoice stays even when March 2027 arrives. Deleting evidence after a duty to preserve it has arisen can bring serious penalties.

Remember that retention applies to every copy, including backups and archives. Backups usually hold data for far less time than archives do, and they should not be treated as a substitute for an archive.

Here is what to take away. Keep data as long as law, contract and business require, and no longer, and let a legal hold override the schedule.

studyNotes.heading: End of life and end of support
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at what happens when products grow old, because the exam expects you to know the difference between two dates.

End of life, or EOL, is when the maker stops making or selling the product. Help may continue for a while. End of support, or EOS, is when the maker stops giving updates and help. No more security fixes will come.

Think about a car model. One year, the factory stops building it. That is like end of life. You can still drive it, and the garage still gets parts. Some years later the parts run out and nobody can repair it. That is like end of support.

EOS is the more dangerous date. After it, a newly found flaw stays unfixed forever. Attackers know this and they look for such systems. Exact dates and even the meaning of the words differ by maker, so read the notice. Some makers also say end of service life.

Here is a worked example. A maker announces end of life for a network switch in June 2027 and end of support in June 2029. A switch is a device that connects computers on a network. The company needs 12 months to plan, buy and install replacements. So it must begin by June 2028 at the very latest, and it should really start sooner and budget for it now. Replacing it all on the day of the notice would be needless panic. Ignoring the notice would be worse.

If an old system must stay after EOS, management should accept the risk formally. Add compensating controls, which are extra protections that reduce the risk, such as separating the system from the network, restricting who can reach it and watching it closely. Treat this as a temporary state with a replacement plan.

Asset retention also means thinking ahead. Keep equipment or software that you need to read old records. A record held for ten years is useless if the only program that opens it has gone.

Think like a manager. Your inventory should show these dates, so that replacement is planned and budgeted, not a surprise.

Here is your takeaway. End of life stops the sales, end of support stops the fixes, so plan to replace before end of support.

studyNotes.heading: Data remanence
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at why removing data is so much harder than it sounds.

Data remanence is data left behind after an attempt to remove it. To remain is to stay, and remanence is what stays.

Deleting and normal formatting usually remove only the pointers to the data. Think of a library drawer full of index cards. If you tear out the card for a book, the book is still on the shelf. Anybody who walks along the shelf can find it. A computer's delete command is much the same. It marks the space as free, and the data sits there until something writes over it.

Different kinds of storage leave data behind in different ways.

A hard disk drive, or HDD, stores data magnetically on spinning platters. A deleted file stays there until it is overwritten. Also, a file may not fill all of the space given to it, and bits of older data can stay in the leftover area, which is called slack space.

A solid-state drive, or SSD, stores data on chips, and it is a special problem. It moves data around to spread wear across its chips. This is called wear leveling. It also keeps spare areas that the computer cannot normally reach. So when you overwrite a file, the drive may write to a different place, and the old copy can stay where it was. Overwriting can therefore miss some copies.

Random access memory, or RAM, is a computer's short-term memory. It can hold data for a short time after power is lost. An attacker with physical access may try to read it in that short period, and this is known as a cold boot attack.

Data also hides in places that people forget. Office printers and copiers often have internal drives that hold images of what was scanned. Phones, network devices and old backup tapes hold data as well.

Here is a workplace example. A company returns a leased copier without thinking about it. The internal drive still holds images of contracts and staff records. Nobody broke in. The data simply left the building inside the machine.

Here is what to take away. Deleting is not removing, SSDs make overwriting unreliable, and any device that stores data must be sanitized before it leaves.

studyNotes.heading: Clear, purge and destroy
studyNotes.body:
Now we come to the three levels of sanitization, and the exam expects you to be exact about what each one means.

Sanitization is the general word for removing data from media, which is anything that stores data, so that it cannot reasonably be recovered. The National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST, a United States standards body, uses three levels, in this order from weakest to strongest.

- Clear: protects against recovery with normal software tools, usually by overwriting.
- Purge: makes recovery infeasible even with laboratory tools.
- Destroy: makes recovery infeasible and also leaves the media unusable.

Below all of these sits ordinary erasing, which is a normal delete. It is not sanitization at all.

Think about a whiteboard. Wiping it with a dry cloth is like erasing. You can still make out the words. Cleaning it properly so nobody in the room can read it is like clearing. Treating it so that no expert could ever bring the words back is like purging. Breaking it up and burning it is like destroying.

Clearing suits reuse inside the organization, at the same level of sensitivity. On a modern magnetic hard disk, one overwriting pass is generally treated as enough. The old advice to overwrite many times comes from much older drives.

Purging suits media that will leave your control or be reused for less sensitive work. Examples are the drive's own secure-erase command, degaussing of magnetic media, and crypto-erase. Note that a purge can leave the device working, as a secure-erase command does, or it can ruin it, as degaussing does to a hard drive. What defines a purge is that laboratory recovery is not feasible.

Destroying means physically ruining the media by shredding, disintegrating, melting or burning. It is the surest method. Choose it for the most sensitive data, and for media that cannot be purged, or when the media is cheap compared with the harm of a leak.

You may also see the word declassification used about media. It means preparing media so that it can be reused at a lower level. If there is any doubt, many organizations refuse to do this.

Here is your takeaway. Erase is not enough. Clear beats software tools, purge beats the laboratory, and destroy leaves nothing to reuse.

studyNotes.heading: Degaussing and crypto-erase: the limits
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look closely at two purge methods, because the exam tests when each one does not work.

Degaussing uses a very strong magnetic field to scramble magnetically stored data. It works only on magnetic media, such as hard disk drives and tapes. It does not work on SSDs, which are solid-state drives that store data as electrical charge on chips. It does not work on optical discs, such as CDs and DVDs, which store data as marks read by a laser. A stronger magnet does not change this.

A simple way to hold on to it is that magnets only beat magnets.

Degaussing has other limits as well. The machine must be strong enough for the type of media, because modern drives resist magnetic fields more strongly than old ones. It usually ruins a hard drive, because the drive's own control information is wiped too. And a hybrid drive, which has both magnetic platters and a memory chip, keeps whatever is on its chip.

Crypto-erase, or cryptographic erasure, means destroying the keys for data that was encrypted. Encrypted data has been scrambled, so that only a key holder can read it. Think of a safe that can never be cracked. If every key is thrown into the sea, the contents are gone for all practical purposes, even though the safe is still there.

Crypto-erase is fast, and it works on SSDs. It is very useful in the cloud, which means computers run by another company, because you cannot touch the disks. Many drives, called self-encrypting drives, do this with one command.

But it only works under certain conditions.

- The encryption must be strong.
- It must have been on from the start.
- Every copy of the key must be gone.

If a laptop ran for a year without encryption, and encryption was turned on later, old data may still sit unencrypted in places such as spare areas. If a copy of the key sits in a recovery safe, or in a backup, then the data can still be read, so that copy must be destroyed and recorded too.

Here is what to take away. Degaussing is for magnetic media only. Crypto-erase needs strong encryption from the start and the end of every copy of the key.

studyNotes.heading: Worked examples: choosing a method
studyNotes.body:
In this final part we will practice choosing a method, and we will see what must happen after the data has gone.

Ask three questions. How sensitive is the data? Will the media leave our control? And what type of media is it? The type matters because it rules some methods out.

Let us work through some cases.

A hard disk drive is being reused in the same department, for data at the same class. Clear it. There is no need to spend more, because the media stays under your control.

A hard drive is being sold to the public, and it must still work afterwards. Purge it, for example by a secure-erase command, then verify. Degaussing would not suit this case, because the buyer would receive a dead drive.

Old laptops with SSDs are being donated. Use the maker's secure-erase or crypto-erase, if the conditions for it are met. Do not degauss.

A box of old DVDs holds confidential files. Shred them, in a machine built for optical discs. Degaussing does nothing to them.

A drive held the most secret data, and it will not be reused. Destroy it. A drive costs very little compared with the harm of a leak.

Data sits on a cloud provider's disks. Crypto-erase it, because you have no physical access.

Paper needs a method too. A cross-cut shredder cuts in two directions, which makes rebuilding a page much harder than with long strips. Pulping and burning are also used for the most sensitive paper.

There are always two steps after the sanitization. First, verify the result, because a tool may fail silently. Second, keep a record, such as a certificate of destruction, which is a signed statement of what was destroyed, when and how.

If a contractor does the work, the responsibility to get it right is still yours. Use an approved company, keep a chain of custody, which is a signed record of who held the media at each handover, and get the certificate. You may also want to watch it happen.

Think like a manager. Choose the method by the sensitivity and the destination, not by habit, and follow your written policy.

Here is your takeaway. Match the method to the sensitivity, the destination and the type of media. Then verify and record.

keyTerms.meaning: An order to keep certain data for a legal matter, overriding normal deletion.
End of Life: the maker stops making or selling a product.
End of Support: the maker stops giving updates and help for a product.
Data left behind on media after an attempt to remove it.
Overwriting data so that normal software tools cannot recover it.
Removing data so that even laboratory methods cannot practically recover it.
Physically ruining media so it can never be used or read again.
Removing data from magnetic media with a very strong magnetic field.
Destroying all copies of the keys so that encrypted data can never be read.
Solid-State Drive: storage that keeps data on chips and has no magnetic disks.

keyPoints: Keep data as long as law and business require, and no longer.
A legal hold overrides normal deletion.
EOS means no more security fixes, so plan replacement before it arrives.
The order from weakest to strongest is clear, purge, destroy.
Degaussing works only on magnetic media, not on SSDs or optical discs.
topics.memoryHook: Clear for here, Purge for leaving, Destroy for the deepest secrets. Magnets only beat magnets.

question.prompt: A charity is donating old laptops to a local school. The laptops have solid-state drives that held donor records. The IT (information technology) lead plans to degauss the drives before handing them over. What is the BEST advice?
options: Use a stronger degaussing machine so that the magnetic field reaches every part of the drive
Use the maker's secure-erase function or crypto-erase, then verify the result and record it
Format each drive twice, because two full formats will remove all of the donor records
Delete the donor folders, empty the recycle bin, and give the laptops to the school
question.explanation: Solid-state drives store data on chips, so a magnetic field does not sanitize them. A purge method such as secure erase or crypto-erase leaves the laptop usable. Degaussing is tempting because it works well on hard disks, but a stronger magnet does not change this. Formatting and deleting leave data behind.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's policy deletes email after three years. Its lawyers report that a lawsuit has begun, and some of the affected email is nearly three years old. What should happen FIRST?
options: Suspend deletion of the relevant email by placing it under a legal hold from the lawyers
Let the deletion run as scheduled, because the written policy has to be followed in every case
Delete the relevant email sooner, so that the company has less to hand over to the other side
Move the relevant email to a personal drive belonging to one of the company's senior lawyers
practiceQuestions.explanation: A legal hold overrides normal deletion until it is lifted. Following the schedule is tempting, since policy usually wins on this exam, but the policy itself gives way to a duty to preserve evidence. Early deletion could bring serious penalties.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has kept every record since it was founded, just in case. A recent breach exposed customer files that were 15 years old and had no remaining use. What is the BEST long-term fix?
options: Buy more storage, so that the old records can be spread over a larger number of encrypted disks
Keep the old records, but move all of them to a folder that most staff do not know exists
Delete everything older than one year at once, without asking what the law or contracts require
Adopt a retention schedule based on law, contracts and real business need for each record type
practiceQuestions.explanation: A retention schedule keeps each type of data for as long as required and no longer. Deleting everything old is tempting because it removes risk quickly, but it could break laws and contracts that require certain records to be kept.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Hard disk drives from an accountant's computer will be reused by another accountant in the same department, at the same class. The drives never leave the company's control. Which option BEST fits?
options: Destroy the drives in an approved shredder and buy new ones
Clear the drives with an approved overwriting software tool
Degauss the drives and put them straight back into service
Delete the accountant's files and empty the recycle bin
practiceQuestions.explanation: Clearing suits reuse inside the organization at the same class. Destruction is tempting because it is the surest method, but it wastes usable drives when the risk is low. Degaussing usually ruins a hard drive, and deleting is not sanitization.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company is selling used hard disk drives that held internal business records. The buyers are members of the public, and the drives must still work after the sale. Which approach is BEST?
options: Reformat each drive with the normal operating system tool and then check that it appears empty
Degauss each drive with a rated machine and then test that it can still be read by a computer
Purge each drive using its own secure-erase command, then verify that the data has gone
Delete all visible folders, then fill the drive with harmless files and delete those files as well
practiceQuestions.explanation: Media leaving the organization's control should be purged, and a secure-erase command leaves the drive usable. Degaussing is tempting because it is a true purge method for hard drives, but it usually ruins them, so the buyer would get a dead drive.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A records office has boxes of old recordable DVDs, which are optical discs, holding confidential case files. A technician offers to run them through the office's degausser. What is the BEST advice?
options: Use the degausser, but run each box through it twice so that the field reaches the inner discs
Erase each disc using the computer's normal delete function and then reuse them as blank discs
Store the discs in a locked room for ten years, after which the data will have faded away
Do not use the degausser at all, and physically shred the discs in a suitable machine
practiceQuestions.explanation: Optical discs do not store data magnetically, so degaussing has no effect, and shredding is the right method. Repeating the degauss is tempting because it sounds thorough, but no amount of magnetism changes marks read by a laser.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A laptop's drive was used without encryption for a year. Full-disk encryption was then turned on, and the laptop will now be given to an outside charity. A technician proposes crypto-erase by destroying the key. What is the BEST advice?
options: It may not be enough, because data written before encryption began may remain unencrypted
It is sufficient, because destroying a key always removes every trace of data from a drive
It is sufficient, provided that the technician also empties the recycle bin before giving it away
It is not needed, because the encryption that was turned on has already erased all earlier data
practiceQuestions.explanation: Crypto-erase depends on encryption having been in place from the start, because data written earlier may remain unencrypted, for example in spare areas of the drive. The second option is tempting, but destroying a key only affects data that the key protects.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company performs crypto-erase on a cloud database by deleting its encryption key from its key management system. Later, a review finds a copy of that key in a recovery safe. What is the MOST important next step?
options: Do nothing, because the copy of the key in the recovery safe is protected by a physical lock
Ask the cloud provider to degauss the disks that hold the company's encrypted database
Destroy that remaining copy of the key as well, and record that it has been destroyed
Move the copy of the key to a different safe in another building that has better locks
practiceQuestions.explanation: Crypto-erase is complete only when every copy of the key has gone, and the record proves it. Moving the key to a better safe is tempting because it adds protection, but the data can still be read for as long as a copy exists.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A maker announces that a network switch has reached end of life and will no longer be sold. Security fixes will continue for three more years. What is the BEST response?
options: Replace every switch this week, because the product became unsafe on the day of the notice
Take no action at all, because the maker will surely extend the support date when the time comes
Buy several spare switches and plan to keep using them for as long as they continue to work
Plan and budget for replacing the switches well before the end of support date arrives
practiceQuestions.explanation: End of life stops sales, while end of support stops the fixes, so the replacement should be planned ahead of the later date. Replacing them this week is tempting because it feels safe, but the switches are still supported and the cost is not justified.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's lease on a multi-function printer is ending, and the leasing firm will collect it next week. The printer scans contracts and holds images of them on an internal drive. What should be done before collection?
options: Clear the print queue shown on the screen and print a test page to confirm that it still works
Sanitize the internal drive using an approved method, and record that it was done
Ask the leasing firm to confirm by telephone that it never looks at returned equipment
Unplug the printer for a full day so that any stored information is lost from its memory
practiceQuestions.explanation: The internal drive holds data remanence and is about to leave the company's control, so it must be sanitized, and that must be recorded. Unplugging is tempting because short-term memory does fade, but an internal drive keeps its data without power.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Hard drives held a company's most valuable trade secrets. They are old, they will not be reused, and they cost very little compared with the harm of a leak. What is the BEST way to dispose of them?
options: Physically destroy them and keep a signed certificate
Clear them with a single overwrite and donate them
Format them and store them in an unlocked cupboard
Give them to the cheapest recycler and trust its care
practiceQuestions.explanation: The data is highly sensitive and the media has no reuse value, so destruction with a record is the right match. Clearing is tempting because it is cheap and quick, but clearing only stops normal software tools, and the drives would then leave the company's control.

topics.name: Data security controls and compliance: data states, scoping and tailoring, standards selection, data protection methods such as DRM, DLP, CASB
topics.simpleExplanation: Data is always in one of three states. It is resting somewhere, moving somewhere, or being used. Each state needs different protection, just as money needs a vault, an armored van, and a careful cashier. Organizations do not invent their controls from nothing. They pick a published standard, remove what does not apply, and adjust the rest to fit. They then add tools that follow sensitive data, watch for leaks, and watch how staff use cloud services.

studyNotes.heading: The three data states
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at the three states that data can be in, because each one needs its own kind of protection.

Think about money. In a vault, it is at rest. In an armored van, it is in transit. And when a cashier is counting it on a counter, it is in use. The vault's thick door does nothing to protect the van, and the van's guards do nothing for the cashier.

Data at rest is stored, as on a disk or a backup tape. Protect it with encryption, which is scrambling so only a key holder can read it, and with access controls and physical locks. The usual encryption choice is the Advanced Encryption Standard, or AES. It can be applied to a whole disk, to a database or to single files.

Data in transit, also called data in motion, is moving across a network. Protect it with Transport Layer Security, or TLS, which secures web traffic, or with a virtual private network, or VPN, which is a protected tunnel across another network.

Data in use is being worked on in a computer's memory or shown on a screen. It is often unencrypted at this moment, so it is the hardest state to protect. Use strict access limits, screen locks and clean desk rules. Newer hardware can keep data protected while it is being processed. This is often called confidential computing, and it relies on a sealed area of the processor known as a trusted execution environment.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital encrypts its disks, which protects data at rest. It uses TLS between the ward computers and the server, which protects data in transit. Then a nurse leaves a patient record open on a screen at the reception desk, where visitors can see it. Neither of those controls helps. That is data in use, and it calls for a privacy filter and an automatic screen lock.

Watch the common mistake. A company proud of its website security may leave its database and backups unencrypted. One state is covered, and another is wide open.

Here is what to take away. Data is at rest, in transit or in use, each state needs its own controls, and data in use is the hardest to protect.

studyNotes.heading: Baselines, scoping and tailoring
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at how organizations adapt a published list of controls to fit, and at two words that the exam loves to swap.

A baseline is a starting list of minimum security controls. A control is anything that reduces risk. It is like a builder's standard checklist for a new house.

Scoping means removing the controls that do not apply. A house with no pool can skip the pool fence rules.

Tailoring means adjusting the remaining controls to fit the organization. A house in a storm area may need stronger windows.

Here is the worked example. A clinic adopts a baseline of 200 controls. It has no wireless network, so it removes 15 wireless controls. That is scoping, and 200 minus 15 leaves 185. The baseline says screens lock after 15 minutes. Ward computers are in public areas, so the clinic changes this to 5 minutes. That is tailoring. The number of controls did not change, only how one of them works.

A simple way to remember it is that scoping cuts, and tailoring fits.

In United States government guidance, scoping is treated as one part of the wider tailoring process. That guidance comes from the National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST. So you may see tailoring used as the bigger word. It can include setting values for controls, adding extra controls, and using compensating controls, which are alternatives used when a normal control cannot be applied. On the exam, when the two words appear side by side, scoping is removing and tailoring is adjusting.

Keep a written reason for every change, and get management approval. An auditor will ask why each control was removed or changed. A sound reason recorded at the time is your answer. An honest shrug is not.

There is one firm limit. Laws and contracts cannot be scoped away. If a health privacy law requires a control, then it stays, however expensive it is. Cost alone is not a reason to scope out a legal duty.

Think like a manager. Scoping and tailoring are decisions about risk, so the right people approve them and the reasons are kept.

Here is your takeaway. Scoping removes what does not apply, tailoring adjusts what is left, record why, and never scope out the law.

studyNotes.heading: Selecting standards
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at how to choose which standards to follow, and at the common names that you should recognize.

Think about opening a small restaurant. First you must follow the health and fire laws. Next you must follow the terms of your lease and your supplier agreements. Then you may choose to follow a respected cookery school's kitchen guidelines, because they help you run things well. The order matters.

Choose in this order.

- First, what you must follow by law or regulation.
- Next, what you must follow by contract.
- Then, voluntary good practice that fits your risks.

Here are examples that you should recognize.

- General Data Protection Regulation, or GDPR: European Union personal data law.
- Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA: United States health data law.
- Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, or PCI DSS: a card industry standard, usually required by contract, for anyone handling payment cards.
- International Organization for Standardization, or ISO, 27001: a standard for running a security management program.
- National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST, Special Publication 800-53: a United States catalog of security controls.
- Center for Internet Security, or CIS, Benchmarks: secure settings for particular products.

A few details are worth holding on to. PCI DSS is not a law, even though it can feel like one. It comes from the card industry and it binds you through your contracts. ISO 27001 is the standard that an organization can be certified against, while its companion ISO 27002 gives guidance on the controls. NIST publishes baselines at low, moderate and high impact, and an organization picks one based on how much harm a loss would cause.

Standards overlap, so many organizations map them together. One control can then satisfy several sets of rules.

Here is a workplace example. An online retailer starts selling to customers in Europe and taking card payments directly. Before anything else, its security manager identifies what the law and contracts require. GDPR and PCI DSS are not optional. Only then does it choose a voluntary framework to organize the work.

Here is what to take away. Law first, then contract, then voluntary good practice that fits your risks.

studyNotes.heading: Digital Rights Management
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the first of three named tools in the outline. It is the one that stays with the file.

Digital Rights Management, or DRM, controls what someone can do with a file they already have, such as view, print, copy or forward. Access can also expire. When used inside companies, it is often called Information Rights Management, or IRM.

Think about renting a film online. You can watch it on your screen, but you cannot copy it for a friend, and after 48 hours it stops playing. You have the file, but the rules came with it.

That is the key difference from ordinary access control. Ordinary access control is like a locked door. Once you are through the door and you have picked up the document, the door no longer matters. DRM is like a document that has its own rules, wherever it travels.

DRM usually works by encrypting the file, and then releasing the key only to permitted people, under stated conditions. Common features include these.

A license says what a particular person may do. A check back to a central server confirms that the license is still valid. An expiry date ends access automatically. An audit record shows who opened the file and when. Some systems also place a visible or hidden mark on the file, called a watermark, so that a leak can be traced.

Here is a workplace example. An engineering firm shares drawings with a partner. The partner can open them, but cannot print or forward them, and access ends on the day the contract ends. If the relationship goes badly, the firm can withdraw access to the copies already sent.

DRM has limits. Someone who can see a file on a screen can still photograph the screen. It needs software on the receiving side, which can frustrate partners. And if the central server is unavailable, permitted people may be locked out, so there is an availability cost.

Pick DRM when the need is to control a file after it has been handed to someone else. If the need is to stop a file leaving at all, that is a different tool, and we turn to it next.

Here is your takeaway. DRM follows the file and controls what people can do with it, even after they have received it.

studyNotes.heading: Data Loss Prevention
studyNotes.body:
In this part we will look at the second tool, which guards the ways out of the organization.

Data Loss Prevention, or DLP, looks for sensitive data, such as card numbers, and alerts on or blocks it when it tries to leave.

Think about the security gate at a shop, or a guard who checks bags as people leave a warehouse. The guard does not care what you did inside. The guard cares about what you are carrying out.

DLP can run in three places, and each one matches a data state.

- On the network: it watches data in transit.
- On staff computers, also called endpoints: it watches data in use.
- In storage: it scans data at rest to find sensitive files.

The placement decides what it can see. Network DLP cannot see a file being copied to a Universal Serial Bus, or USB, storage stick, because that copy never crosses the network. Endpoint DLP can see it. Storage DLP is valuable for finding sensitive files in places where they should not be.

How does it recognize sensitive data? It may look for patterns, such as the format of a card number. It may look for particular words. It may compare files with exact fingerprints of known sensitive documents. And it may read the class label in a file's metadata, which is the data about the file. This is another reason why classification comes first. DLP can only protect what it can recognize.

DLP has a well-known blind spot. Encrypted traffic can hide data from it. If an employee uploads a file to a personal website over an encrypted connection, network DLP may see nothing at all. The fix is to inspect encrypted traffic at an approved point, or to use DLP on the staff computers, where the data can be seen before it is encrypted.

False alarms are the other challenge. A rule that is too broad blocks honest work. So many organizations begin by only alerting, tune the rules, and then begin to block.

Here is a workplace example. A bank's email system stops a message containing 300 account numbers, and tells the sender and the security team.

Here is what to take away. DLP guards the exits, the placement decides what it sees, and encrypted traffic can blind it.

studyNotes.heading: CASB, and methods that change the data
studyNotes.body:
In this final part we will look at the third tool, and then at methods that change the data itself.

A Cloud Access Security Broker, or CASB, sits between users and cloud services, which are online services run by another company. It shows which services are used, including unapproved ones, and applies rules to them.

Think of a building's reception desk. Everyone going to any office passes it. It knows who goes where, and it can stop someone carrying what they should not.

A CASB can work in two ways. Inline means it sits in the path of the traffic, so it can act at the moment an upload happens. The other way uses a software connection into the cloud service itself, often called an application programming interface, or API. That way, it can inspect data already stored there, but it usually acts after the event.

A typical need is to stop files labeled Restricted being uploaded from home computers, while allowing the service for other work. That is a job for a CASB.

Other methods change the data itself.

Masking hides parts of it, as on a receipt showing only the last four card digits.

Tokenization swaps it for a meaningless stand-in value called a token. The real value is kept in a secure vault. A retailer's order systems can hold only tokens, so a breach of those systems exposes nothing usable.

Pseudonymization replaces names and other details with codes, and the link between them is kept separately. Because the link exists, the data can be traced back to the person, so it is still personal data under privacy law.

Anonymization removes the link permanently, so that nobody can be identified. Truly anonymous data falls outside privacy law such as the General Data Protection Regulation, the European Union law. Doing it properly is harder than it sounds, because combined facts can often identify someone.

Pick by the need. DRM, which is Digital Rights Management, follows the file. DLP, which is Data Loss Prevention, guards the exits. And CASB watches the cloud.

Think like an adviser. Start from what must be protected, and where it is, and only then choose the tool.

Here is your takeaway. CASB controls cloud use, masking hides, tokens replace, and pseudonymized data is still personal data.

keyTerms.meaning: Data that is stored, such as on a disk or tape.
Data moving across a network. Also called data in motion.
Data being worked on in memory or shown on a screen.
A starting list of minimum security controls.
Removing the baseline controls that do not apply to you.
Adjusting the remaining controls to fit your organization.
Digital Rights Management: controls what a person can do with a file they already have.
Data Loss Prevention: finds sensitive data and alerts on or blocks it when it tries to leave.
Cloud Access Security Broker: sits between users and cloud services to see use and apply rules.
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: security rules for anyone handling payment cards.

keyPoints: Data is at rest, in transit or in use, and each state needs its own controls.
Data in use is the hardest state to protect.
Scoping removes what does not apply, and tailoring adjusts what is left.
Meet law and contract needs first, then choose voluntary standards.
DRM follows the file, DLP guards the exits, and CASB watches the cloud.
topics.memoryHook: Vault, van, cashier: at rest, in transit, in use. Scoping cuts, tailoring fits.

question.prompt: A design firm shares drawings with outside partners. The partners should be able to open the drawings, but not print or forward them, and their access must stop when the contract ends. Which control BEST meets this need?
options: Data Loss Prevention on the firm's outgoing email and network connections
A Cloud Access Security Broker placed between the firm's staff and its cloud services
Full-disk encryption on every computer the firm's own designers use
Digital Rights Management applied to the drawing files
question.explanation: Digital Rights Management stays with the file and controls what the partner can do after receiving it, including expiry. Data Loss Prevention is tempting, but it guards the firm's own exits and cannot limit a partner's printer. The other two do not control a file once it is in a partner's hands.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A nurse has a patient's record open on a screen at a reception desk, where visitors can see it. The hospital's disks are encrypted and its network traffic is protected. Which state of data is exposed, and which control BEST fits it?
options: Data at rest, which calls for a stronger encryption setting on the disks in the reception computer
Data in transit, which calls for a private network link between the reception desk and the server
Data in use, which calls for a privacy filter and an automatic lock on the reception screen
Data at rest, which calls for a review of who can enter the data center holding the patient records
practiceQuestions.explanation: Data shown on a screen is in use, and disk or network encryption does nothing for it. Data at rest is tempting because the record is stored somewhere, but the exposure here comes from its being displayed.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An auditor confirms that a shop's website protects all traffic with Transport Layer Security. The same auditor finds that the customer database and its backups are stored without encryption. Which data state is MOST clearly unprotected?
options: Data in transit
Data at rest
Data in use
Data in motion
practiceQuestions.explanation: Stored databases and backups are data at rest. Data in use is tempting because a database is busy all the time, but the finding is about how the data is stored. Data in motion is another name for data in transit.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A clinic is applying a baseline of controls. One control is expensive, and it is required by the health privacy law that applies to the clinic. A manager wants to scope it out. What is the BEST advice?
options: Remove it, and write down the cost as the reason for doing so in the records of the baseline
Remove it, provided that senior management signs a form accepting the risk of breaking the law
Remove it for now, and then add it back in if a regulator happens to ask about it at an inspection
Keep it, because a control that the law requires does apply and cannot be scoped out
practiceQuestions.explanation: Scoping removes controls that do not apply, and a control required by law does apply. Formal risk acceptance is tempting because it is the usual route for risk decisions, but management cannot accept away a legal duty.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A team adopted a published baseline and removed or changed many of its controls. When an auditor asks why, nobody can explain the changes. What is the BEST corrective action?
options: Document the reason for each change, and obtain management approval for each one
Return to the full baseline at once and apply each control exactly, whether it is relevant or not
Tell the auditor that baselines are only advice, and so no record of the changes is ever needed
Choose a different published baseline so that the auditor's questions about this one fall away
practiceQuestions.explanation: Changes to a baseline need a recorded reason and management approval. Returning to the full baseline is tempting because it removes the question, but it would apply controls that do not fit and would waste money.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A growing online retailer begins selling to customers in Europe and accepting card payments directly. It wants to choose which security standards to adopt. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Adopt the most popular voluntary framework, then check whether it also happens to meet any laws
Ask the web development team which standards it would find the easiest to put into practice
Identify which laws and contracts bind the company in each of its new markets
Buy the security product that advertises compliance with the largest number of different standards
practiceQuestions.explanation: Legal and contract duties are not optional, so they are identified first, and voluntary standards follow. Adopting a popular framework is tempting because it gives a quick structure, but it may not satisfy what the retailer is actually bound to do.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company approves one cloud storage service. It wants to stop staff uploading files labeled Restricted from unmanaged home computers at the moment the upload happens, while allowing other use of the service. Which control BEST meets this need?
options: Full-disk encryption on each laptop that the company owns and manages
A Cloud Access Security Broker that works inline on each upload
A written policy sent by email to all staff once each quarter
A firewall rule that allows all traffic to the approved service
practiceQuestions.explanation: An inline broker sits in the path of the traffic and can apply rules to each upload as it happens. A firewall rule is tempting because it controls traffic, but it sees only where the traffic is going, and it knows nothing of the label on a file.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A research team replaces patient names with codes and keeps the table linking codes to names in a separate secure system. A manager says the data is now anonymous, so privacy law no longer applies. What is the BEST response?
options: Agree, because replacing a name with a code always removes the data from all privacy laws
Agree, as long as the table that links the codes to the names is kept in a locked server room
Disagree, because a record that contains a code must always be treated as Top Secret
Disagree, because the data is only pseudonymized and can still be linked back to patients
practiceQuestions.explanation: While the link exists, the data can be traced back to a person, so it is pseudonymized and remains personal data. Keeping the table locked is tempting because it is good security, but it does not make the data anonymous.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's network Data Loss Prevention tool catches card numbers in ordinary email. An employee then uploads a file of card numbers to a personal website over an encrypted connection, and the tool sees nothing. What would BEST close this gap?
options: Turn the tool off, because it has shown that it cannot catch every attempt to send data out
Ask all staff to agree that they will never use encrypted websites while they are at work
Inspect encrypted traffic at an approved point, or add the tool on staff computers
Buy a second network tool of the same type, and place it beside the first one on the same link
practiceQuestions.explanation: Encryption hides the content from a network tool, so the data must be examined where it can be seen. A second network tool is tempting because it sounds like extra coverage, but it would be just as blind.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company wants to stop staff copying customer lists from their laptops to USB (Universal Serial Bus) storage sticks. The copying never crosses the network. Which control BEST fits?
options: Network Data Loss Prevention on the link to the internet
Endpoint Data Loss Prevention running on staff computers
A Cloud Access Security Broker in front of cloud services
Transport Layer Security on all of the web servers
practiceQuestions.explanation: Endpoint tools run on the computer where the copying happens, so they can see it and block it. Network Data Loss Prevention is tempting because it is the same type of tool, but a copy to a USB stick never passes through the network.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A retailer wants to keep card numbers out of its own order systems, so that a breach of those systems exposes nothing usable and fewer systems fall under the card industry's rules. Which method BEST meets this goal?
options: Tokenization, with real numbers held in a secure vault
Masking the card number on all of the cashiers' screens
Digital Rights Management on all of the exported reports
Stronger passwords for all of the order system's users
practiceQuestions.explanation: Tokenization replaces the card number with a meaningless value, and the real number stays in a secure vault. Masking is tempting because it also hides digits, but the full number would still be held behind the screen.

examQuestions.prompt: A school's shared server holds thousands of public newsletters and one folder of student medical notes, which is at the school's highest class. The principal asks for lighter, cheaper protection, because almost all the files are public. What is the BEST advice?
options: Protect the server at the level of most of its files, because public files are the majority
Protect the server at a middle level as a fair balance between cost and risk
Protect it at the level of its most sensitive file, or move that folder elsewhere
Keep the lower level and ask all staff to sign a promise not to open the medical folder
examQuestions.explanation: A system takes the level of the most sensitive data it holds. Moving the folder is a good business option, because the server could then be protected at a lower cost. A middle level sounds reasonable, but it under-protects the medical notes.

examQuestions.prompt: A company has built a new customer database. The database administrator asks who should decide its classification. The head of sales is the senior manager accountable for customer information. Who should make the decision?
options: The head of sales, who is accountable for the customer information
The database administrator, who knows exactly where the data is stored and how it is backed up
The security manager, who is responsible for the risks across the whole organization
The internal auditor, who can give an independent view of the correct level
examQuestions.explanation: The data owner is the accountable business manager and sets the class. The administrator is the custodian and carries out the rules. The security manager is tempting and can advise, but the decision belongs to the owner. An auditor must stay independent.

examQuestions.prompt: A cleaner finds a USB (Universal Serial Bus) storage stick with no marking on the floor of a bank's restricted records room. What should happen FIRST?
options: Open it on an isolated computer so staff can decide which class it belongs to
Mark it as Public until a member of staff comes forward to claim it
Wipe it at once so that nothing on it can possibly leak out of the bank
Give it to the security team and treat it as the highest class
examQuestions.explanation: An unmarked item is treated as the highest class until the facts are known, and security staff follow the proper process. Opening it on an isolated computer is tempting, but it skips that process. Wiping it destroys evidence of what happened.

examQuestions.prompt: A project manager has a deadline today. She wants to change a report from Confidential to Public so it can go to a supplier by ordinary email. The report still contains current pricing. What should the security adviser recommend?
options: Allow the change this one time, and record it as an exception for the next audit to look at
Keep the class and use the approved secure method, since only the owner may change it
Remove the marking from the report and send it without any class shown at all
Ask the email team to place the supplier's address on a list of trusted contacts
examQuestions.explanation: The content has not changed, so the class should not change, and the decision belongs to the owner anyway. An exception sounds like a practical manager's choice, but a deadline does not reduce the harm of exposing current prices.

examQuestions.prompt: A serious flaw is announced in a widely used web server product. The security team needs five days just to learn which of the company's systems use it. Which action would BEST fix the underlying problem?
options: Keep an accurate inventory with named owners, updated by automated discovery
Subscribe to a faster alert service for news of flaws
Hire more analysts to check every system by hand
Patch all servers automatically on each release
examQuestions.explanation: The cause is that the company does not know what it has, so an accurate inventory fixes the cause. Faster alerts and more analysts treat symptoms. Automatic patching is tempting, but untested updates can break systems, and unknown systems would still be missed.

examQuestions.prompt: An online shop in Europe plans to move its customer records to a cheaper cloud location in another country, to cut costs. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Test whether customers will notice any slowdown in the website after the move
Encrypt the records, because encrypted data is free of any rules on where it is kept
Check what the law and customer contracts allow for keeping the data in that country
Ask the cloud provider's sales team to confirm in an email that the location is suitable
examQuestions.explanation: The location of personal data can carry legal limits, so the law and contracts come first. Encryption is tempting and is a good control, but it does not remove those legal duties. A sales team cannot give the organization legal assurance.

examQuestions.prompt: A factory's machine controller runs software whose maker ended all support last year. No more security fixes will come. A replacement cannot arrive for 14 months, and the factory cannot run without the machine. What is the BEST approach?
options: Keep it running as it is, because it has been stable for years and has never had an incident
Shut the machine down today and stop the factory until the replacement has finally arrived
Ask the operators to take extra care and to report anything strange that they happen to notice
Isolate it, add compensating controls, and have management formally accept the risk
examQuestions.explanation: The business must keep running, and the risk must be reduced and owned by management. Past stability is tempting, but it says nothing about future attacks on a system that can no longer be fixed. Shutting down harms the business more than the risk requires.

examQuestions.prompt: A company is ending its contract with a cloud storage provider. The company cannot reach the provider's physical disks. Its data was strongly encrypted from the first day, using keys that only the company controls. What is the BEST way to sanitize the data?
options: Ask the provider to degauss all of its disks
Destroy every copy of the encryption keys and record that this was done
Delete the files and rely on the provider's recycling
Overwrite each file once through the web console
examQuestions.explanation: Crypto-erase fits the cloud, because it needs no physical access and the data cannot be read without the keys. Overwriting through the console is tempting, but the customer cannot confirm that all copies were reached. Providers do not degauss shared disks for one customer.

examQuestions.prompt: A small clinic adopts a published list of security controls. It has no wireless network, so it removes the wireless controls. It also shortens the screen lock time on computers in public areas from 15 minutes to 5. Which statement BEST describes these two actions?
options: Removing the wireless controls is tailoring, and changing the lock time is scoping
Both actions are scoping, because each one makes the list smaller for the clinic
Removing the wireless controls is scoping, and changing the lock time is tailoring
Both actions are risk transfer, because each one changes who must carry the risk
examQuestions.explanation: Scoping removes controls that do not apply, and tailoring adjusts the remaining ones to fit. The swapped option is tempting because the two words are so close. Changing the lock time does not remove any control, so it is not scoping.

examQuestions.prompt: Staff at a company are using many cloud applications that were never approved. Management wants to see which applications are in use and apply company rules to uploads into approved ones, without stopping cloud use altogether. Which solution BEST meets this goal?
options: A Cloud Access Security Broker placed between staff and their cloud services
Digital Rights Management applied to every document that staff create or receive at work
A firewall rule blocking all outbound traffic to every known cloud service address
Full-disk encryption on all of the laptops and desktop computers that staff use
examQuestions.explanation: A Cloud Access Security Broker sits between users and cloud services, shows what is used, and applies rules. Blocking is tempting, but management does not want cloud use stopped, and it gives no view of how approved services are used. The other two do not show cloud use.

reviewSession.heading: Classifying information and assets: objective 2.1
reviewSession.body: Let us go back over Domain 2 together, one objective at a time, starting with classification. Classification sorts things by the harm that exposure, change or loss would cause, so that the cost of protection matches the value. The order to remember is management support and policy, find what you have, name an owner, classify, protect, then train and review. The owner chooses the class, and technical staff carry it out. People mix up the word Confidential, because it is the lowest secret government level and often the highest company level. They also forget that an asset takes the class of the most sensitive item on it. Government levels from the top are Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, Unclassified. When an answer offers to buy a tool before you know what you hold, it is usually wrong.

reviewSession.heading: Handling rules: objective 2.2
reviewSession.body: Now for handling. Rules are written per class, and they cover marking, storage, use, transport and disposal. The protection follows the information into every copy and every format, so a backup needs the same care as the original. Marking is for people to read, and a label is for machines. Mark public items too, so that a missing mark stands out, and treat anything unmarked as the highest class until the owner confirms it. In transport, encrypt, seal, and keep a chain of custody, which is a signed record of who held the item. Keep the class off the outer wrapping of highly sensitive items. Keep keys apart from the data. The favorite trap is lowering a class to meet a deadline. Only the owner may change a class, and convenience is never the reason.

reviewSession.heading: Provisioning, ownership and inventory: objective 2.3
reviewSession.body: Next comes secure provisioning. Give people only what the job needs. Need to know decides which information they may see, and least privilege decides what they may do with it. The owner approves, the technical team carries out, and the rights come back when the job changes. Owners can delegate the work, but they keep the accountability. An asset with no owner is an asset nobody protects, so have management name one. The inventory must hold tangible assets, which you can touch, and intangible ones, such as data, licenses and patents. People forget the intangible half, and it is often worth the most. When a discovery scan disagrees with the list, investigate first. And if an audit finds things missing, choose the answer that fixes the process, not the answer that buys replacements.

reviewSession.heading: The six data roles: objective 2.4
reviewSession.body: This is the most tested part of the domain, so let us be exact. The owner is a senior manager who is accountable, sets the class and decides on access. The custodian, usually technical staff, carries out the daily care, such as backups. The user follows the rules. Those three are found inside the organization. The controller decides why and how personal data is used. The processor is a separate party that follows the controller's instructions. The subject is the living person the data is about. People wrongly call an internal technical team a processor, when it is a custodian. A processor that decides purposes for itself is treated as a controller for that use. Hiring a processor never ends the controller's accountability. If a question asks who decides, look for the owner or the controller.

reviewSession.heading: Lifecycle, collection, location and maintenance: objective 2.4
reviewSession.body: Let us review the lifecycle. The six stages are create or collect, store, use, share, archive and destroy, and the class travels with the data throughout. On collection, gather only what you need for a stated purpose, tell people why, have a lawful basis, and do not quietly reuse data for something new. The best control for unneeded data is not to have it, so be wary of answers that encrypt what should never have been collected. On location, data sovereignty is about whose law applies, and data residency is about where data must sit. Check backups as well as the main copy, and check the law and contracts before moving anything. Encryption does not cancel those rules. On maintenance, keep data accurate, review access, patch systems, recheck the class, and test your restores.

reviewSession.heading: Retention and product age: objectives 2.4 and 2.5
reviewSession.body: Now retention. Keep data as long as law, contract and business need require, and no longer. Destroying too early and keeping too long can both break the law. A legal hold overrides normal deletion until it is lifted, even when the written policy says to delete. On product age, end of life means the maker stops making or selling the product. End of support means the maker stops giving updates, so no more security fixes will come. End of support is the more dangerous date, and replacement should be planned and budgeted before it. If an old system has to stay, the best answer combines isolation or other compensating controls with formal risk acceptance by management. Do not choose an answer that keeps it running because it has always been stable, or one that shuts the business down.

reviewSession.heading: Remanence and the three sanitization levels: objective 2.4
reviewSession.body: Let us go over removing data. Data remanence is what is left behind after an attempt to remove it. Deleting and normal formatting usually remove only the pointers, so neither one is sanitization. The three levels, from weakest to strongest, are clear, purge and destroy. Clearing defeats normal software tools, and it suits reuse inside the organization at the same class. Purging makes recovery infeasible even in a laboratory, and it suits media leaving your control. Destroying also leaves the media unusable, and it suits the most sensitive data. People assume that a purge always ruins a device, but a secure-erase command leaves the drive working. To choose, ask how sensitive the data is, whether the media will leave your control, and what type of media it is. Then verify the result and keep a record.

reviewSession.heading: Degaussing, crypto-erase and solid-state drives
reviewSession.body: These two methods have limits that the exam loves. Degaussing uses a strong magnetic field, and it works only on magnetic media, such as hard disk drives and tapes. It does nothing to solid-state drives, which store data on chips, or to optical discs. A stronger machine does not change that. It also usually ruins a hard drive, so it cannot be the answer when the drive must keep working. Solid-state drives move data around and keep spare areas, so overwriting can miss copies. Use the maker's secure-erase function, crypto-erase, or physical destruction. Crypto-erase means destroying the keys, and it needs strong encryption from the start and the removal of every copy of the key, including any in a recovery safe. It is the natural answer for cloud storage, where you cannot touch the disks.

reviewSession.heading: Data states, scoping and tailoring: objective 2.6
reviewSession.body: Now objective 2.6. Data is at rest when stored, in transit when moving across a network, and in use when in memory or on a screen. Data in use is the hardest to protect, and disk or network encryption does nothing for a record on a visible screen. A baseline is a starting list of minimum controls. Scoping removes the controls that do not apply. Tailoring adjusts what is left to fit. So scoping cuts and tailoring fits, and the exam will try to swap them. In United States government guidance, tailoring is the wider word that includes scoping. Keep a written reason and management approval for each change, and remember that a legal duty cannot be scoped out. When choosing standards, law comes first, then contract, then voluntary good practice. Payment card rules usually bind you through contracts, not law.

reviewSession.heading: Choosing between DRM, DLP and CASB: objective 2.6
reviewSession.body: Let us finish the tools. Digital Rights Management, or DRM, follows the file, and controls what someone can do after receiving it. Data Loss Prevention, or DLP, guards the exits, and looks for sensitive data trying to leave. It can run on the network, on staff computers or in storage, and encrypted traffic can hide data from it. A Cloud Access Security Broker, or CASB, sits between users and cloud services, shows what is being used, and applies rules. So read the need closely. If a partner already has the file, choose DRM. If something must not leave, choose DLP. If the concern is unapproved or uncontrolled cloud use, choose CASB. Remember too that masking hides, tokenization swaps data for a stand-in, and pseudonymized data is still personal data, because it can be linked back.

reviewSession.heading: How to choose the best answer in this domain
reviewSession.body: Here is how to think when a Domain 2 question looks hard. First, ask who should decide. Very often the right answer is the owner, and the tempting answer is a capable technical person. Second, ask what comes first. Knowing what you have comes before buying tools, and checking the law comes before moving data. Third, look for the cause. If a process is failing, fix the process and do not just treat the single event. Fourth, match the protection to the value, so be cautious of answers that protect everything the same way. Fifth, check the media type before choosing a sanitization method. And finally, think like a manager and adviser. People's safety comes first, then follow policy and the law, and make sure that the right person has made and recorded the decision.
